These verses also continue the commentary on the hypocrites, addressing their words, actions and intentions. They reveal their inner intentions, which they had carefully taken pains to conceal, but they could not hide them. They object to the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) distribution of sadaqat (obligatory charity). How could a Muslim possibly criticise the justice of the Messenger (ﷺ)? He is infallible and possesses an exalted character. Some of them also say of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he is a person who lends his ear to everyone, believing every person to be truthful. Yet the Prophet (ﷺ) is a prophet and a person of insight, a thinker and a statesman, and he has been given the treasures of wisdom. Some of them conceal their disbelieving and sinful beliefs and deeds very well, but when their deception is exposed they take refuge in false oaths so that they can conceal their affairs and actions. Others remain so fearful and anxious that a surah might be revealed about them concerning the Prophet (ﷺ).

In commenting on such people, it is made clear that these are the characteristics of hypocrites, and that there is no difference between them and the hypocrites who came before them. Just as Allah destroyed the hypocrites of earlier times, He will destroy them too, and just as Allah granted respite to those earlier hypocrites, so respite is being granted to them, so that it becomes known who the lying hypocrites are and what sincere believers are like.

﴿If they are given something from it, they are pleased; but if they are not given from it, behold, they become angry.﴾ When they are given something, they are delighted, and then they show no concern for justice and their religious zeal is not stirred. There are many narrations concerning the revelation of these verses, in which specific individuals are identified who objected to the Prophet's (ﷺ) just distribution of sadaqat.

Bukhari and Nasa'i have narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was busy distributing sadaqat when Dhul-Khuwaysirah al-Tamimi came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, be just!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! If I am not just, who will be just?" At that point Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to strike off his head." Upon this the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave him alone. He has companions whose prayers you would regard as trivial compared to your prayer, and whose fasts you would regard as trivial compared to your fast. They will pass out of the religion just as an arrow passes swiftly out of its bow." Abu Sa'id said: At that time this verse was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who criticise you concerning the sadaqat﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh has narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) began distributing the spoils of Hunayn, I heard a man saying: 'This is a distribution that was not made for the sake of Allah.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him. He said: 'May Allah have mercy on Musa; he was harmed even more than this and he showed patience.'" At that time this verse was revealed: ﴿And among them are those who criticise you concerning the sadaqat﴾.

Ibn Jarir has narrated from Dawud ibn Asim, who said: Sadaqat came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he distributed them on the spot, giving something to one person and something to another. An Ansari saw this and said: "This is not a just distribution." At that time this verse was revealed.

Qatadah says that the phrase ﴿And among them are those who criticise you concerning the sadaqat﴾ means that some of them find fault with you regarding the sadaqat. The narrations report that a man who had only recently arrived from the countryside saw the Prophet (ﷺ) distributing gold and silver, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, if Allah has commanded you to be just, then you have not been just." Upon this the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! If I am not just, who will be just?"

In any case, the verse clearly states that this remark came from the hypocrites. They did not say it out of religious zeal; rather, they considered themselves more deserving, or, if they were not given anything on some occasion, they lost their temper. This was clear evidence of their hypocrisy, because if a person is a true believer in the religion of Islam and has certainty, he cannot harbour such an ill opinion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Moreover, the Prophet (ﷺ) was known as "the truthful and trustworthy" even before his prophethood. Especially since justice is the duty of all the people of faith, how much more so should it be expected of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who must not be unjust. These verses also show that they comment on events and matters that had already taken place, and that some of them had happened even before the Battle of Tabuk. Yet they are included here so that it may be known what the lasting characteristics of the hypocrites are and what their mentality is. On this occasion the Noble Qur'an tells the people of faith how their conduct ought to be.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 59:

﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّهُمْ رَضُوا...﴾ etc. How good it would have been if they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them, and had said: "Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and His Messenger too will bestow upon us. To Allah alone do we turn our hopes."

This is the way of thinking in Islam, this is the manner of speech in Islam, and these are the etiquettes of faith in Islam. That a person should be content with the distribution of Allah and His Messenger, and bow his head in submission before the commands of Allah and His Messenger. It should not be that he obeys only out of pressure or because the environment overwhelms him. Trusting in Allah is the etiquette of Islam, for Allah alone is sufficient for His servants. A person should keep hoping for the bounty of Allah and His Messenger, and should do every deed purely for the pleasure of Allah, with no material gain before him. No worldly greed should be in his sight. These are the etiquettes of faith through which a person's heart and conscience are refreshed and filled with joy. The hearts of the hypocrites and their conduct are devoid of and unacquainted with these etiquettes, because the freshness and joy of faith never enter their souls, and their hearts are empty of the light of certainty.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 60:

After the explanation of the proper etiquette before Allah and His Messenger, that is, complete obedience, complete obedience, complete submission and acceptance, and complete surrender, it is stated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not act of his own accord in whatever he does. He carries out every task by the command of Allah. The divine injunctions regarding the distribution of charities are these, and the Messenger follows these injunctions, and these injunctions are from the Lord of the Worlds. That is, charity and zakat are an obligation levied on the wealthy, and it is also obligatory that it be distributed among the poor. Its distribution is to be carried out among several categories of people. No one has the authority to distribute it at his own discretion. Even the Messenger of Allah cannot distribute it at his own discretion beyond these categories.

Through this verse, Islamic Shariah gives zakat a fundamental importance. Now zakat is no longer mere voluntary charity or voluntary donation. Now it is a definite obligation and a compulsory tax. Moreover, it will not be considered a gift from those who distribute zakat, nor a gift from those who give it, but a known obligation. It is an important financial obligation of the Islamic state. There will be a system for its collection, and a code for its distribution has also been put into effect. In short, it is an obligation upon those who give zakat, and a right for those who receive it. It is not charity or begging, because Islam does not permit anyone to receive zakat with the notion of begging.

In the Islamic order, life is founded on action and striving. The concept of action is very broad. It is the duty and responsibility of the Islamic state to arrange employment for every person who is capable of action and labour, to teach him skills for work and provide him with opportunity, and then to guarantee to the labourer and the worker that he will receive the full wage of his labour.

According to the rules of the Islamic system, those who are capable of action have no claim on zakat. Zakat is a tax that is taken from the wealthy and given to the needy, and its collection and distribution remain in the hands of the government, provided the government is founded on Islamic principles, enforces the system of Shariah, and collects and spends zakat in full accordance with complete Islamic rules.

Hadith: Hazrat Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that the Messenger of Allah said: "Lā taḥillu aṣ-ṣadaqah li-ghaniyyin wa lā li-dhī mirratin sawiyy" — "Zakat is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who is healthy and strong." (Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi)

Abdullah ibn Adi ibn Khiyar narrates that two men told him that they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and requested zakat. The Messenger ﷺ looked at them and saw that both were healthy and strong, and said: "If you wish, I will give you zakat, but according to the rule, there is no share in it for the wealthy, nor for a person who is capable and able to earn." (Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Nasa'i)

The social system of Islam has proposed a social security system for Islamic society, of which zakat is one part. This system is broader and more comprehensive than zakat, because Islam's social security system has many branches. These branches extend over the entire span of human life. Zakat, nevertheless, is an important part of this system.

The rate of zakat is one-tenth, one-twentieth, and one-fortieth. Its rate differs among different kinds of wealth. A person who holds wealth exceeding 20 Egyptian dinars, and whose wealth is more than his needs, is considered a person of the nisab (threshold), and zakat becomes obligatory upon him. In this way, a large number of contributors is provided in this category, and it is spent on the categories explicitly mentioned in this verse. The first to deserve it are the poor (fuqara') and the needy (masakin). The fuqara' are those who have less than what is needed, and the masakin are likewise, but they are, in comparison with the fuqara', people of outward affluence. They do not express their need and do not ask.

This tax is so wide that one who gives zakat in one year may also become its recipient in another year, if the income of the zakat-giver falls below his needs. In this respect, it is an excellent collective fund. There are also some people who never make any payment into this fund, yet they are certainly entitled to it; in this respect it is a collective guarantee. But even before it becomes a collective fund or guarantee, it is an obligation from Allah. Through it, the soul and wealth are purified. A person worships Allah, the miserliness of the heart is removed from him, and a person finds joy in giving, and a sense of superiority is not produced within him.

The Categories of Zakat

1. Al-fuqara' wal-masakin (the poor and the needy). We have already explained the definition and difference between faqir and miskin.

2. Wal-'amilina 'alayha (those employed to collect the charities).

3. Wal-mu'allafati qulubuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled).

There are several kinds of those whose hearts are to be reconciled. Those who had only recently entered Islam, and whose support from this category had the aim that they remain steadfast upon Islam. Among them are also those whose hearts are to be reconciled in order to bring them into Islam. Among them are also those who entered Islam with firm conviction, but to whom rewards and honours were given so that their people would receive the impression that they too should incline towards Islam, when they see that their brothers are benefiting from the blessings of the Islamic system. Regarding this category, there are juristic differences among the jurists as to whether the category of mu'allafat al-qulub remained after the victory of Islam or not. But the activist nature of Islam requires that this category continues, because in various circumstances, workers of the Islamic movement suffer financial losses due to the movement, and their remedy is necessary, and sometimes Islam benefits from reconciling certain people. It is a great divine wisdom that Allah has provided Muslims with this special fund to resolve their problems, so that it may be benefited from in various circumstances and conditions.

5. Wa fi al-riqab (in freeing necks). This refers to a time when slavery was a global system, and this system was prevalent both among Muslims and their opponents, because prisoners of war were made slaves. Islam, in the international circumstances of that time, was compelled to make decisions regarding prisoners that corresponded to what was being done to its own prisoners. This category also included assistance to those who entered into a mukatabah (contract of manumission) with their master by agreeing on a price for freedom. Such people were given money from zakat to pay the instalments of their mukatabah. Moreover, from the funds of this category, slaves were also purchased and freed, that is, by the Islamic government.

6. Wal-gharimin (in aid of debtors). Debtors who did not incur debt through wrongdoing. Money was paid to these people from zakat so that they could pay off their debts. Today's modern economic systems, which are products of so-called Western civilisation, are so oppressive that they take people's loans and devour them, and very easily declare themselves bankrupt, and people's sums are lost. But Islam is an interdependent and guaranteeing system. In it, the noble cannot be easily plundered, nor are trustees permitted to be destroyed and bankrupted in this way, nor are people permitted to devour one another's wealth. And laws do not make the way smooth for such people themselves, whereas today, under all the financial laws of the world, this happens.

7. Wa fi sabil Allah (and in the way of Allah). This is a broad category. Expenditure may be made from it on every occasion in which there is benefit to the Islamic society, as is evident from the breadth of the expression fi sabil Allah.

8. Wabn al-sabil (in hospitality to the traveller). That is, a traveller who is away from his wealth, even if he is wealthy in his own place.

This is the system of zakat, which some people in today's age criticise, alleging that it is a system of begging, of benefaction, and of dependence upon others. Yet it is a collective obligation, performed as an Islamic duty and act of worship, so that people's wealth may be purified and the rust of miserliness may be cleared from people's hearts. And this system should become a cause of people's welfare and of love and brotherhood among the individuals of the Ummah. The atmosphere of human society should be refreshed by it, and it should serve as a balm for the wounds of humanity. And along with these blessings, it also provides a broad arrangement of social security. But its true colour should remain worship and nearness to Allah, and it should be a link between Allah and people. A obligation from Allah (fariḍatan min Allah) — and Allah imposed these injunctions because He is wise and knowing. Wallahu 'alimun hakim (Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 61:

After laying down the principles of zakat and sadaqat and identifying their beneficiaries, the discourse now turns again to the conduct and actions of the hypocrites. The verse about sadaqat has been brought here so that the weakness of the position of those who found fault with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the distribution of sadaqat may become clear.

﴿And among them are those who hurt the Prophet and say, "He is all ears."﴾ Meaning: "Among them are some who hurt the Prophet by their words and say that this man is credulous, believing whatever he hears."

This is an open insult and a clear disrespect towards the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It appears that this insult was in addition to the matter of sadaqat. They observed how graciously, nobly and seriously the Messenger of Allah ﷺ listened to people's words, and that he dealt with people according to their outward condition, in accordance with the law of the Shariah. He attended well to people and spoke to them with an open heart. But these fault-finders interpreted this courtesy of the Messenger as a weakness, and called goodness evil. They said that the Messenger is credulous, that is, he listens to everyone, and it is possible that someone may lie to him, deceive him, and gain his ends through smooth talk, and he would not be able to understand the matter. They said these things because of their own vain imagination, that the Messenger might uncover their affairs in some way, or that he would find out their hypocrisy through some means. It is also possible that they found fault with the situation in which the sincere believers gave the Messenger information about the words and deeds of these hypocrites, and he believed them. Some narrations of this kind are also reported concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. Both of these matters may be the background of this verse, since both existed among the hypocrites.

The Qur'an first quotes their saying: "They say, he is all ears." (They say that this man is credulous. Yes, this is true, but say: it is for your good.) Is it not for your good that he listens attentively to revelation and then conveys to you what is good for you and what reforms you? Moreover, his being credulous is better for you in that he listens to your words attentively and with nobility, and does not give you the impression that you are hypocrites. He does not even hint that you deceive, and although he knows of your hypocritical conduct, he does not rebuke you.

﴿He believes in Allah﴾ and Allah informs him about you, and he has complete certainty in that information. He is also certain of the information given to him about other people.

﴿And believes the believers﴾ He accepts their words as true with complete reassurance, because he knows that they are true Muslims, and their faith is so firm that it restrains them from lying, hypocrisy and pretence.

﴿And a mercy for those of you who believe﴾ Because Allah is Ghayur (jealous of His honour). How could He tolerate that people hurt His Messenger, although he is the one who conveys the message of Allah to them?

These people swear oaths before you in order to please you, and this has always been the way of the hypocrites in every age. They always say one thing and do another: their conduct in front of you is different, and their conduct behind your back is different. Then there comes a time when they cannot even meet the eyes of the sincere believers, nor can they speak with them. So they take refuge in oaths and, through flattery and humiliation, seek the approval of people.

But if they are truly believers, then Allah and His Messenger deserve far more that they should strive to please them, for what is the standing of people? What is the status of people? The reality, however, is that one who does not believe in Allah and does not bow before Him, believes in people and fears his fellow human beings. It would have been better for them to bow before Allah, who is the God of all. In that there is no humiliation for them. Humiliation lies in a person bowing before a fellow human being. One who fears Allah is not a liar; rather, one who fears others besides Allah is a liar.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 63:

This interrogative is one of denial, and the intended purpose is to rebuke and warn the addressees: these people profess faith, and yet they wage hostility and war against Allah and His Messenger. Therefore they should know that waging war against Allah and His Messenger is a grave sin, and that the one who harbours enmity against Allah and His Messenger, Hell awaits him. And for this arrogance and rebellion of theirs, they will be given the punishment of humiliation and disgrace. If they are truly believers, as they claim to be, then how is it possible that they should be unaware of this reality?

They fear the servants of Allah, and out of fear they swear false oaths so that they may please them and deny the reports that are reaching these servants concerning them. But it is astonishing that they do not fear the Creator of the universe, so that they torment His Messenger and act with enmity toward His religion. As if they fight against Allah, and His power is so supreme that no one can fight against Him. Rather, they commit a shameful sin, and what they are doing is a great error, and it is extremely dangerous for them that they plot against the religion and cause harm to the Messenger of Allah.

These people are so cowardly that they cannot come out openly against the religion, its adherents, and the Messenger of Allah. Then they also fear that Allah may reveal their secrets even to the believers, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may be informed of their concealed intentions.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verses 64–66:

The hypocrites are wary (Ayat 64 to 66). These verses comment on the general attitude of all hypocrites: they are constantly afraid that verses may be revealed about the defect in their hearts, and that their inner condition may be exposed. Their secrets may be disclosed to the people. Several narrations describe specific incidents on this subject, stating that these particular incidents are the occasions of revelation of these verses.

Abu Ma'shar al-Madani narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. He said: one of the hypocrites said that, in his view, those among us who recite the Qur'an most are the most greedy for food, the most untruthful in speech, and the most cowardly at the time of war. (His remark was about those who were reciters of the Qur'an.) This statement reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So this hypocrite came to the Messenger of Allah. At that time the Messenger of Allah had mounted his she-camel to set out on a journey. The hypocrite said: "O Messenger of Allah, we were only chatting and passing the time." Then the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Were you mocking Allah, His verses and His Messenger?" At that moment these verses were revealed: "Say: Was it Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking? ... they were criminals." The feet of that man were being dragged over stones, and the Messenger of Allah was not even looking at him, and this man was hanging on to the saddle-strap of the Messenger of Allah.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq has related that there was a group of hypocrites, among whom were Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, a brother of Banu Umayyah, the son of Zayd, the son of Amr, the son of Awf, and a man named Makhshi ibn Humayr, who was from the tribe of Ashja', and Ashja' was an ally of Banu Salimah. This group was going with the Messenger (ﷺ) towards Tabuk. Some of them said to others: "Do you think that the Romans fight the way Arabs fight one another? By Allah, we see that tomorrow you will all be bound in ropes." They said this to spread fear among the believers. At this point Makhshi ibn Humayr said: "By Allah, I propose for myself that a hundred lashes be inflicted on each of us, but let not the Qur'an be revealed because of your words." Among the reports that reached me is also this: the Messenger (ﷺ) instructed Ammar ibn Yasir: "Go to these people, for they have fallen into Hell, and ask them what they were saying. If they deny it, then tell them: you did say it." Ammar went to them and spoke to them about this. These people came to the Messenger of Allah and began to make excuses. The Messenger of Allah had already mounted his riding animal, and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit arrived, holding the saddle of the camel, and was saying: "We were only chatting and passing the time." Makhshi ibn Humayr said to the Messenger of Allah: "Give me a new name and change my father's name." Thus, in this verse, the one who received pardon was Makhshi ibn Humayr. Afterwards he named himself Abdur Rahman, and he asked Allah that he be martyred in the way of Allah in such a manner that not even his trace would be known. Accordingly, in the Battle of Yamamah he was martyred, and no trace of him was found.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was preparing for the expedition of Tabuk, and with him was a group of hypocrites who said: "Does this man hope that the palaces and fortresses of Syria will open for him? That is impossible." Allah informed the Messenger (ﷺ) of this, so he ordered that the mounts of these people be stopped. The Messenger went to them and asked whether they had said this. They replied: "O Messenger of Allah, we were only joking and playing." Then these verses were revealed concerning them.

"We were only joking" means that the subjects they were discussing were connected with the very foundations of faith, and these were not matters to be spoken of in the manner of idle chatter. "Say: Was it Allah, His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?" Since they had committed a grave offence, a ruling of disbelief was passed upon them, for they had uttered words of unbelief and, after professing faith, had disbelieved. Thus they are warned of a dreadful end. However, if they repent quickly and truly embrace faith, this punishment may be averted from them. But those who remained in hypocrisy and continued in their mocking manner will deserve the punishment, because "they were criminals."

The hypocrites are wary (Ayat 64 to 66). These verses comment on the general attitude of all hypocrites: they are constantly afraid that verses may be revealed about the defect in their hearts, and that their inner condition may be exposed. Their secrets may be disclosed to the people. Several narrations describe specific incidents on this subject, stating that these particular incidents are the occasions of revelation of these verses.

He said: one of the hypocrites said that, in his view, those among us who recite the Qur'an most are the most greedy for food, the most untruthful in speech, and the most cowardly at the time of war. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 67:

After commenting in detail on the hypocrites' thoughts, deeds and statements, the commentary now points out the general reality of the hypocrites. Their common characteristics are described, on account of which they appear distinct from the truly faithful believers, and it is explained what kind of punishment awaits them.

The hypocrites, both men and women, share one and the same nature and constitution. Their temperament is also uniform. In every age and place, and always, these have been their features. Although their words and deeds differ, they are derived from one and the same temperament and one and the same source, namely spite and bad nature, carrying out secret conspiracies, making baseless criticisms, shrinking from coming out into the open, and lacking the courage to speak openly. These are the real signs of the hypocrites. Now, what is their conduct? They enjoin what is evil (munkar) and forbid what is good (ma'ruf), and they are extremely stingy. And if they spend, they spend only to be seen by people. And when they do enjoin what is evil and forbid what is good, they do it secretly and furtively. They continue their activities through hints and innuendo, because they do not have the courage to act openly. They act openly only when they are certain that the circumstances are favorable and that there is no danger to them. They have forgotten Allah and His pleasure: ﴿نَسُوا اللَّهَ﴾ (They forgot Allah). Therefore the aim and purpose of all their actions is the pleasure of people or worldly gain. When these people do not fear God, then they fear the powerful people of the earth very much. They remain humiliated before them and flatter them. Therefore Allah has also forgotten them: ﴿فَنَسِيَهُمْ﴾ (so He has forgotten them). Therefore now they have no weight or standing. They will be without weight and without standing in the eyes of people in this world, and they will be without weight and without standing with Allah in the Hereafter. Because in this world people do value those who are bold and powerful, who speak plainly and openly, who hold to their convictions, and who confront people over their convictions. If they wage war, they do so openly, and if they make peace, they do so openly. These people forget people and remember the Lord of the worlds (ilaha al-'alamin), so they do not fear the reproach of any reproacher in the matter of truth. And since they remember Allah, people remember them and esteem them.

Surely the hypocrites are the transgressors: ﴿إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾. Therefore they are outside the circle of faith. They have deviated from the true path, and Allah has prescribed for them the same end that has been prescribed for the disbelievers.
So this outcome is sufficient for them and for their criminal conduct. Alongside this outcome and Hell, they will also continue to be cursed, and they will remain forever in this punishment.

The hypocrites' class, which is inactive, deviant and misguided, has always existed in human history. It has never been unique at any time. Even before Islam, examples of it have existed in human history, and the end of the hypocrites of earlier eras has likewise been in accordance with their wickedness and depravity. This is because a crookedness comes into the nature of such people, and they do not walk on the right path. The disbelievers and hypocrites who passed before were possessed of more wealth and greater manpower than the hypocrites of the Prophet's (ﷺ) time. But these material and manpower resources could not save them.

The Qur'an, pointing to the hypocrites of earlier nations, tells them: Look, you are walking on the very path of these people. Why, then, should your end be different from theirs?

The temptation of power is also a dangerous temptation. A person falls into temptation through material and manpower strength. Those whose connection is with a great power do not take smaller powers into account; they fear only a stronger power. Therefore they render obedience and submission to that great power and strive to raise the word of that great power. Material and manpower strength does not affect such people, because they know that it is Allah who gives wealth, property, helpers and children, and He is the supreme power. Therefore, if blessing comes to them, they are very eager to give thanks, and they expend their material and manpower strength in obedience to Allah. As for those whose nature has deviation, and who do not know what the source of this power is, they adopt arrogance, pride and rebellion, and they confine their activities to eating and drinking, just as cattle eat and drink.

﴿They are those whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and they are the losers.﴾

The voiding of deeds means that their deeds became invalid from their very foundation, because they were like a plant without roots. Such a plant neither becomes green nor flourishes, and those who plant such a plant end up in loss, and their loss is all-encompassing.

Now that the hypocrites are set aside, the address becomes general. This general address is made in a tone of wonder: how strange these people are, that despite seeing and knowing the end of earlier peoples, they still continue on the same path.

These people are enjoying the pleasures of this world, and they have no proper awareness of their own condition. They keep walking continuously on the path of destruction and do not take any advice to heart.

﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them?﴾ "Has not the history of those who came before them reached them?" Those who walked the same path that they are walking on. Just read the history of the people of Noah, how the flood overtook them and they were destroyed, and that was a terrible destruction. The people of 'Ad, who were seized by a violent wind. The people of Thamud, who were destroyed by a mighty shriek and sound. The people of Abraham (peace be upon him), who were composed of great tyrants; Allah destroyed them and, miraculously, granted salvation to Abraham. The companions of Madyan, whom a severe earthquake seized. And the people of Lot, whose offspring Allah cut off and left, with only a few people escaping that punishment. Do these people not know these historical events? Messengers came to those nations too, bringing clear proofs. But those nations denied them unjustly, and Allah seized them.

﴿And Allah was not one to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ "So it was not Allah's act to wrong them, but they themselves were the ones who wronged themselves." A deviant person is made even more rebellious by power and authority. Then, because of wealth and property, such people become blind. Therefore, the historical events of the past benefit only those whose eyes of insight are open and who have the capacity to understand the Sunnah of Allah, because the Sunnah of Allah is unchangeable and always operates, and it grants no one any exemption. Many of those who are given power, authority, and favours, and who are put to the test, become blind; the sight and insight of their faculties are veiled, and they remain unable to perceive realities. They cannot see how great powers in history were brought low. Most people do not reflect on the end of these rebels and tyrants. When a person renders himself blind and deaf in this way, he becomes deserving of Allah's punishment. Now the Sunnah of Allah does its work, and the principle of the recompense of deeds comes into play, and such people and nations are seized. They are proud of their strength, and, becoming insolent through blessings and luxuries, they remain heedless, and suddenly they find themselves encircled by Allah.

The truth is that heedlessness, ignorance, and blindness cling to wealth and property, and their outcome is never good in any age; and those who escape this evil end are only those upon whom Allah's special grace rests.

The hostile front of the hypocrites and disbelievers, and where it will end up, stands in contrast to the believers and the truthful. Their temperament is entirely different from that of the hypocrites and disbelievers. Their conduct is the exact reverse of theirs, and their final outcome is also completely different from theirs.

If the hypocrites are friends of one another, share one nature and have one temperament, then the believing men and believing women also share one temperament and one set of convictions, and are loving friends of one another. Yet the hypocrites, despite being alike in disposition and kind, are not as close-knit as the believers, because friendship can exist only among those who are brave, who come to one another's aid, and who are mutual helpers and supporters, whereas hypocrisy is by its very nature the opposite of these qualities. For in the face of courage, the hypocrite is cowardly and base. They are not sympathetic to one another, nor are they bound together, nor are they mutual helpers and guarantors, even though their thoughts and conduct resemble one another. The Qur'an adopts a somewhat different style for each of the two. For the hypocrites, it uses only the words ﴿ba'duhum min ba'd﴾ (they are of one another), while for the people of faith it uses the words that they are friends of one another: ﴿ba'duhum awliya'u ba'd﴾. The temperament of a believer is the temperament of the community of believers; he has a collective mind. He is united, mutually supportive and helpful, and this unity and mutual support is for the attainment of good and the repelling of evil.

﴿وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتُ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلِيَاءُ بَعْضٍ ۚ يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ﴾ "The believing men and believing women are friends of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong." These goals, namely attaining good and defending against evil, are so lofty and difficult that they require a community that is one in spirit and two in heart. Its members must love and help one another, stand together in one rank against evil, and there must be no factor of division, separation or disagreement among them. When division arises within the community of Muslims, there will inevitably enter into the community some element that is contrary to its temperament, that does not accord with its convictions, and it is through that very element that division enters the community. Because of division, diseases and disorders then arise within the community, and it no longer keeps before it the purpose that is its true aim, nor does it retain within itself the first row of the ummah, namely ﴿ba'duhum awliya'u ba'd﴾. In short, it is because of this quality, that is, the quality of friendship, that the community of Muslims performs its duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and it rises up in the world to raise high the word of Allah. ﴿وَيُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ﴾ "And they establish prayer": the establishment of prayer is its sign.

﴿وَيُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ "And they give zakat": the giving of zakat is the duty that binds the members of the community together, and through it spiritual and physical ties arise among the members of the community, and they advance towards their goal.

﴿وَيُطِيعُونَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ﴾ "And they obey Allah and His Messenger": this is the true objective of a believer. Therefore, for them there is no law or rule other than the command of Allah and the command of the Messenger, and no constitution other than the Shari'ah of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger, and no system other than the religion of Allah and His Messenger. When Allah and His Messenger decide a matter, they do not raise objections or hesitate. Before them there is one path, the straight path, and they do not rush towards the byways of this or that. ﴿أُولَٰئِكَ سَيَرْحَمُهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ "Those are the ones upon whom Allah will have mercy." This mercy is not confined to the Hereafter alone. Its beginning is already in this world, and this mercy also falls upon the individual who performs the duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil and who establishes prayer and pays zakat. And upon the community formed of such individuals, too, the rain of mercy falls. This mercy takes the form of tranquillity of hearts, and also the form of a connection with Allah, and the form of protection from calamities and trials; and it takes the form of the reform of the community, its steadfastness and tranquillity, and mutual love and solidarity among its members; and it also takes the form of the emergence of sincerity and the pleasure of Allah.

These four qualities of the believers stand in opposition to the four qualities of the hypocrites. The qualities of the believers are enjoining good, forbidding evil, performing prayer, and giving zakat. The qualities of the hypocrites are forbidding good, enjoining evil, forgetting Allah, and being miserly. The result is that the mercy of Allah descends upon the believers, while for the hypocrites there is a curse in exchange for these qualities. And as a result of these qualities, Allah has promised the believers that they will be granted victory, triumph, and authority and supremacy upon the earth, so that they may be the righteous and reforming guardians of all humanity.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾ "Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise." He has the power to make the community of believers friends of one another, to bestow honour upon them, and then they perform the commands and obligations of Allah. He is Wise, and through His wisdom He supports this community and grants it honour, so that this community, upon coming to power, may carry out reform in the earth and safeguard the word of Allah among the people.

On one side, the punishment of Hell awaits the hypocrites and disbelievers, and the curse and blame of Allah lie in ambush for them. And this threat is also a torment to their souls: that Allah will cause them to forget themselves. On the other side, there are the means of joy for the people of faith, and these everlasting joys await them.

This group will dwell in those gardens with honour. But for them the greatest reward is the pleasure of Allah, and Paradise with all its comforts is nothing compared to this great reward. And this joy, the joy of the pleasure of Allah, is the greatest joy.

The highest station of nearness to Allah is attained by a person when Allah becomes visible to him, as with his own eyes, that is, the state of shuhud (direct witnessing). In this station a person rises above the impurities of the world, its anxieties and its attachments. In this station a light emerges from the depths of the human heart. Human eyes cannot see this light; this light is the light of Allah, and it is connected with the Spirit of Allah. This station is granted to an extremely small number of people. A single moment and a single flash of this station is more precious than all the wealth and possessions of a whole lifetime. Yet the station of Allah's pleasure is higher still than this, and in it the cup of a person's soul overflows, and the person continually finds the awareness of it within himself.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 73:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) showed great gentleness toward the hypocrites (munafiqin). For a long period he overlooked them and turned a blind eye to their conduct. But now the measure of patience has overflowed. Good manners too have a limit. A command has now come from the Lord, the Holy One, that a certain seriousness should be introduced into his dealings with these people. Now they should be treated in the manner in which the disbelievers (kuffar) are treated, and the command is given that jihad be applied to both of them, and that a harsh attitude be adopted toward them in which there is no softness.

The Islamic movement (tahrik-i-Islami) faces many stages. On some occasions gentleness is necessary, and in some circumstances it is beneficial to be firm. When the period of gentleness has ended and firmness is required, then firmness is necessary. Patience too is for a particular period; when the measure of patience overflows, then the period of firmness begins. This is because the movement faces various circumstances, and different circumstances have different requirements. Through gentleness and granting respite upon respite, at times the situation only deteriorates further.

Among the scholars of knowledge a difference of opinion has arisen regarding harshness toward the hypocrites and jihad against them. One view is that harshness should be shown toward them, as is narrated from Hadrat Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), and Ibn Jarir (rahimahullah) preferred this view. The second view is that they should be exposed in society and treated harshly in their conduct, as is related from Hadrat Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger (ﷺ) did not kill any hypocrite.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 74:

This verse records the general condition of the hypocrites. Their general stance is usually of this kind. From this it is apparent that these people were constantly busy plotting against the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims, but some narrations also mention a specific cause and incident for the revelation of these verses.

Qatadah has said that it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The incident was that a fight broke out between a man from Juhaynah and an Ansari, and the Juhani gained the upper hand over the Ansari. Upon this, Abdullah said to the Ansar, "You do not help your brother." By Allah, the example of us and Muhammad is like the saying, "Fatten your dog so that it may devour you." He further said, "Let us return to Madinah, where the honourable among us will expel the lowly ones." This statement was conveyed to the Messenger of Allah by a Muslim. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Abdullah, he began to swear oaths that he had not said this. Upon this, this verse was revealed.

Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn Jarir narrated with his chain that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting in the shade of a tree, and he said, "A man will come to you who will look at you with the eyes of a devil. When he comes, let no one speak to him." Shortly afterwards, a man with blue eyes appeared before them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called him and said, "On what do you and your companions act?" The man went and brought his companions, and they all began to swear that they had not said these things. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) overlooked them, and upon this this verse was revealed: "They swear by Allah that they did not say it" (yahlifuna billahi ma qalu).

Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and others have narrated, the summary of which is that this verse was revealed concerning Jalas ibn al-Samit. He had a foster-son who was the son of his wife, whose name was Umayr ibn Sa'd. Jalas said that if what has been revealed to Muhammad is true, then we are worse than the donkeys upon which we ride. Upon this, Umayr said, "Jalas, I love you more than all people, and in my view you are a great hero, and I cannot bear that any harm should come to you. But you have said this thing: if I disclose it, it will bring me shame, and if I conceal it, I will be destroyed myself. One of these two situations is bearable for me." So he informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of this matter. But Jalas denied it and swore an oath. Upon this, this verse was revealed. Then Jalas said, "I did indeed say this, but Allah has left room for repentance for me. Therefore I repent," and his repentance was accepted.

However, all these narrations conflict with the words of the Qur'an, wa hammu bima lam yanalu, "and they intended something but could not achieve it." This shows that the narrations are complicated. The reference is to the incident that occurred on the return from the Battle of Tabuk. Some hypocrites wished to suddenly and secretly kill the Messenger of Allah. Among the narrations, we adopt here the following one.

....

Imam Ahmad narrated through Yazid, Walid ibn Abdullah ibn Jumay', and Abu Tufayl. They say that when the Messenger of Allah was returning from Tabuk, he ordered the herald to announce that he was going to pass through a narrow mountain pass, so no one should pass along that path. The reins of the Messenger of Allah's mount were in the hand of Hudhayfah, and Ammar was driving it, when some people came on their mounts wearing masks. They overpowered Ammar, who was driving the Prophet's mount. Ammar arrived and turned the faces of those mounts away. The Messenger of Allah said to Hudhayfah (stop, stop), until the Messenger of Allah dismounted and Ammar returned. Then the Messenger asked Ammar whether he had recognised these people. He said, "I recognised all the mounts, but the people were masked." The Messenger said that these people wanted to startle the Messenger's mount and throw the Messenger down. Ammar asked each of the Messenger's companions how many riders there were on the night of al-'Aqabah. They said there were fourteen, so Ammar said, "If you were among them, then they were fifteen." It is said that the Messenger of Allah identified three of them, and they swore that they had not heard the Messenger's herald's announcement and did not know what the people intended. Upon this, Ammar said, "The remaining twelve were at war with Allah and His Messenger, both in this world and in the Hereafter."

Does this incident indicate what those people's intentions were? Whatever the case, whether this verse refers to this incident or to some other incident, it is clear that such spiteful people still existed among the Muslims. Therefore, the verse expresses wonder at their attitude.

Wa ma naqamu illa an aghnahumu Allahu wa rasuluhu min fadlihi: "Their entire resentment is only because Allah and His Messenger enriched them by His bounty." In short, Islam had not wronged them in any way that would have caused them to seek this retribution. If any harm was done to them, it was only that after Islam, they had been made wealthy and became comfortable, and it was due to this comfortable state that they engaged in these excesses.

After this wonder, which is both astonishing and meaningful, a decisive statement is made.

Fa in yatubu yakhayran lahum, wa in yatawallaw yu'adhdhibhumu Allahu adhaban aliman fi al-dunya wal-akhirah, wa ma lahum fi al-ardi min waliyyin wa la nasir: "Now, if they turn back from this course, it will be better for them; and if they do not turn back, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment, both in this world and in the Hereafter, and there will be none on earth to be their supporter or helper."

Despite these actions, the door of repentance remains fully open. So whoever desires his own good should rush in and enter, and whoever still wishes to walk the crooked path, the outcome is clear: in this world and the Hereafter he will be afflicted with a painful punishment, and in this world he will have no protector or helper. Therefore, if anyone adopts this path, it is he himself who will be blameworthy.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verses 75–77:

The discourse continues in its course, and the features of the hypocrites are coming into view. Their deeds and words are being commented upon.

Among the hypocrites there were some people who had made a covenant with Allah that if Allah bestowed wealth upon them, they would spend lavishly in the way of Allah and do good deeds. But this covenant was made in conditions of poverty and destitution, and at a time when there was hope of receiving something. However, when Allah fulfilled their desire, these people forgot their promises. These people adopted stinginess and miserliness and withheld their hands. Rather, they began to rebel against fulfilling the covenant, as if they had never made any covenant at all. Thus, because of breaking their promise and then lying, Allah firmly planted hypocrisy in the hearts of such people. These people remained hypocrites until the end and met a bad end.

The human soul is very stingy. Only those whom Allah saves escape from it. Only those whose hearts are overflowing with faith can be saved from miserliness. They raise themselves above worldly needs, spurn all greed and self-interest, and their eyes are fixed on the covenant of the Hereafter. The pleasure of the Creator is their aim. They are content because of their faith, and they do not fear becoming poor through spending, because they are certain that whatever a person has is perishable, and whatever is in the treasury of Allah is everlasting. This is the outlook that urges a person to spend in the way of Allah, and a person spends wealth joyfully. A believer holds the conviction that even if wealth leaves his hand, the reward of the Hereafter is still a great reward.

But when a person's heart is empty of faith, he naturally becomes stingy. Whenever he is called upon to spend in the way of Allah, he is miserly out of fear of poverty and withholds his hand, yet he never finds peace and rest. He remains restless forever. The one who makes a covenant with Allah and then violates it, and who lies to Allah, cannot be truthful with anyone. His heart cannot be free of hypocrisy, and the three signs of hypocrisy which the Messenger (ﷺ) specified are: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; and when a trust is placed with him, he betrays it.

Thus, the consequence of breaking covenants and lying about Allah can only be that hypocrisy is imposed upon such people, and they reach that end according to the decision of the verse.

﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾ The result was that, because of their breach of the covenant they made with Allah, and because of the lies they kept telling, Allah planted hypocrisy in their hearts, which will not leave them alone until the day of their appearance before Him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 78:

Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private counsel, and that Allah is the Knower of all hidden things? Despite their claim of faith, do they not know that Allah is aware of the hearts of people, of the thoughts that pass through their minds, of what they say to one another, and of the secret things they discuss? Allah knows the most hidden of matters and the intentions of hearts. They know this well, yet they conceal and still break their promises. This is itself contrary to the demands of their knowledge. The demand of their knowledge was that they should neither hide anything, nor break promises, nor fabricate lies against Allah.

Several narrations are related about the occasion of revelation of this verse. From among them we cite the narration of Ibn Jarir, who, together with Ibn Abi Hatim, related it from Mu'awiyah, who related it from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who related it from Tha'labah ibn Hatib al-Ansari, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray that he be granted abundant wealth. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tha'labah, a little wealth whose thanks you can render is better than much wealth whose thanks you cannot render." It is said that he asked again, and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Are you not content to be like the Prophet of Allah? By Allah, if I wished that mountains become gold and silver for me, they would become so." He again asked, saying: "By Allah, if you pray for me and Allah grants me abundant wealth, I will give to everyone with a right his due from it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, give Tha'labah wealth." It is said that he began to rear sheep, and they multiplied like worms, until Medina could no longer contain them. So he moved away from Medina to a valley and would pray Zuhr and Asr in congregation, while the other prayers were abandoned. Then his wealth increased further and he went so far away that he would attend only the Friday prayer. This wealth kept growing as worms grow, until he also abandoned the Friday prayer. Now he would meet the riders who were going to pray Friday, in order to inquire about affairs. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then said: "What has happened to Tha'labah?" He was informed that he had acquired sheep, that Medina could no longer contain them, that he had therefore moved far away, and they related his condition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tha'labah is ruined, Tha'labah is ruined, Tha'labah is ruined." After this, the command of Allah was revealed: "Take from their wealth a charity" (Khudh min amwalihim sadaqah), and the rules of zakat were revealed. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent two Muslims to collect zakat, one from Juhaynah and the other from Sulaym. He gave them written instructions on how they should collect zakat from the Muslims, and particularly instructed them to go to Tha'labah and a certain man (this certain man was a person from Banu Sulaym) and collect zakat from them. These two first came to Tha'labah, demanded zakat from him, and read aloud the order of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Tha'labah said: "This is merely a jizyah, or the sister of jizyah. I do not understand what it is. Go, and come to me after you have finished with the other people." The Sulaymi man, on hearing this order, set aside some very good camels from his herd for zakat and awaited the agents of the Messenger of Allah. When they saw those camels, they said: "Zakat of such fine camels is not obligatory upon you, so we cannot accept them." The man said: "Take these camels. I am giving them with a willing heart. They are for them." So they took the camels, and while collecting from the other people, they came again to Tha'labah. He said: "Show me your order." When he heard the order of the Messenger of Allah read, he again said: "This is jizyah, or the sister of jizyah. Go; I will think it over and decide." These people came to the Messenger of Allah, and when he saw them he said: "He is ruined." He informed them before they had spoken, and he prayed for blessing for the Sulaymi. These people related to the Messenger of Allah the account of both Tha'labah and the Sulaymi. Then Allah revealed this verse: "And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah..." At that time, a man from Tha'labah's relatives was sitting with the Messenger of Allah. He heard all of this. He set out from Medina, met Tha'labah, and said to him: "Tha'labah, you are ruined. Verses have been revealed concerning you." Tha'labah came to the Messenger of Allah and requested that he accept his zakat. The Messenger of Allah said: "Allah has forbidden me to accept your zakat." Tha'labah began throwing dust on his own head. The Messenger of Allah said: "This is your own doing. I advised you, but you did not heed my words." When the Messenger of Allah refused to take zakat from him, he returned to his dwelling. Then the Messenger of Allah passed away without having taken zakat from him. Then came the period of Abu Bakr, and Tha'labah requested him: "You know my relationship with the Messenger of Allah and my standing among the Ansar; accept my zakat." Abu Bakr said: "Since the Messenger of Allah did not accept your zakat, I cannot accept it." So Abu Bakr never took zakat from him during his lifetime. Then after him, Umar became caliph, and Tha'labah also came to him with his zakat and requested: "O Commander of the Faithful, accept my zakat." He said: "The Messenger did not accept it, Abu Bakr did not accept it; how can I accept it?" So he too died without taking zakat from him. When Uthman became caliph, Tha'labah came to him and requested that he take his zakat. So he too said that the Messenger did not accept it, Abu Bakr did not accept it, Umar did not accept it; should I take it? So he too did not take it. Thus, in the time of Uthman's caliphate, he died.

Whether the revelation of these verses is connected with this incident or with some other incident, the verse is in any case general and points to a general condition. This verse portrays the psychological state of a person who is afflicted with doubt and in whose heart and mind faith has not yet settled. If the occasion of revelation is this, then we would say that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he knew that Tha'labah would remain a hypocrite until death, therefore did not accept his zakat, and did not deal with him according to the general legal principle. The general legal principle is that hypocrites are dealt with according to their outward appearance. Since in Tha'labah's case the Messenger of Allah had been given special information by Allah, he dealt with him in a severely disciplinary manner so that it would be a lesson for others. Thus he was not declared an apostate, so that he could be punished for apostasy, and yet, considering him a Muslim, his zakat was not accepted. This does not mean that according to the Shari'ah zakat is not obligatory upon a hypocrite, since the Shari'ah deals with such people according to their outward appearance; in the matter under discussion, a Prophet had special knowledge. No one else may analogize from this and adopt such conduct.

These narrations also show how the Muslims of the early period viewed zakat. They believed it to be a mercy from Allah upon them. Whoever was deprived of paying it, or whose zakat was not accepted from him, had, as it were, been deprived of a great good; he was so deprived and so at a loss that people began to pity him. The Muslims of the first generations understood the meaning of this verse well.

"Take from their wealth a charity, by which you purify them and cause them to grow" (Khudh min amwalihim sadaqatan tuhhiruhum wa tuzakkihim biha). According to them, zakat was a spoil of war (ghanimah), not a tax which would be a penalty upon them. Therefore, there is a great difference between the financial obligation imposed by Allah, which seeks Allah's pleasure, and the financial obligation imposed upon people by coercion.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 79:

Let us see a glimpse of the two ideas: what the hypocrites held about zakat, and what the sincere believers thought about zakat and charity (sadaqat).

The hypocrites used to mock the charity of sincere and poor believers.

This verse, "Those who find fault with those who give charity voluntarily (alladhina yalmizuna al-mutawwi'in...)," also has a particular occasion of revelation, which shows what the corrupted disposition of the hypocrites thought about spending in the way of Allah.

Ibn Jarir reported through Yahya ibn Kathir and Sa'id ibn Qatadah, and Ibn Abi Hatim through Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrimah (the wording of the narrations differs), that they said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encouraged people to contribute for the expedition to Tabuk. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf gave four thousand (dirhams). He said: "O Messenger of Allah, my total property is eight thousand; I have brought half of it, and I have left half." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah bless you in what you gave and in what you kept back."

Abu 'Aqil brought one sa' of dates and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I earned two sa' of dates. One sa' I give to Allah as a loan, and one I have left for my children." The hypocrites mocked both of them. About 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf they said that he gave so much only to show off, and about Abu 'Aqil they said: "What need did Allah and His Messenger have for one sa'?"

In another narration it comes that they said about Abu 'Aqil: "This man wants to make himself remembered without any reason, whereas he worked the whole night for wages, earned two sa', and presented one sa' before the Messenger."

The hypocrites used to speak in this kind of way about the believers, although they were sacrificing with heart and soul, spending with a willing spirit, and giving to the fund according to what was in their lot, as their share in the struggle. But the understanding of the hypocrites did not reach the sincerity of the Muslims and their pure feelings. Their hearts were extinguished, so they could not perceive the sensitive hearts of the Muslims. They could not grasp the eagerness of the Muslims that they showed in spending in the way of Allah. They offered whatever they gave, little or much, as the result of a faith-driven impulse, and these people were deprived of that faith-driven impulse. Therefore, what else could they say than: if someone gives more, he is a show-off, and if he gives little, he is seeking to have his name written down? If anyone gave more, he was guilty; and if anyone gave less, he was also guilty. Hence, a sound mind would not accept their criticism. This is because they personally were those who stayed behind from jihad, those who dug holes from behind (secretly undermining the believers), and were not ready to give anything for the sake of jihad. If they gave anything at all, it was merely to maintain outward appearance, with an evil intention, and due to base and contemptible motives.

So Allah also gives them an excellent reply: "Allah mocks them, and for them is a painful punishment" (Sakhira Allahu minhum wa lahum 'adhabun alim). Allah mocks those who mock, and for them is a painful punishment. What a dreadful end this is, and what a dreadful mockery it will be from the Creator. On one side is a small group, weak and feeble, humble and perishable; and on the other side is the Creator of the universe and His painful punishment. How terrifying the punishment is to which this weak and feeble human being presents himself.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 80:

These hypocrites, who used to mock the sincere and volunteering believers, saying, "Why do these people spend their wealth?", their end is that even seeking forgiveness on their behalf by the Messenger himself will not benefit them. From this verse it is understood that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), out of his compassion, used to seek forgiveness for these wrongdoers too, perhaps Allah would forgive them.

But Allah has made clear about these people that the end of these hypocrites is settled. No change in it is possible. These people have deviated from the right path, therefore it is not even possible for them to reach a good end. Their hearts have become so corrupt that their reform is not possible.

Therefore the Messenger is told that even if he seeks forgiveness for them seventy times, it will be of no benefit. "Seventy times" does not mean a fixed number; it means abundance, that is, there is no hope of their forgiveness at all. Because the door of repentance has been closed for them. Because when the human heart goes beyond a certain limit of immorality and corruption, then there is no hope of reform left, and when a person goes beyond limits in misguidance, then there is no hope of his returning to the straight path. And Allah is fully aware of the conditions of hearts.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 81:

The context now turns once again to those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah, that is, at the critical stage of the Battle of Tabuk.

The offence of those who stayed behind arose from worldliness. They preferred ease and comfort. They held back from spending in the way of Allah. Weakness of resolve, lack of honour, lack of faith, and a feeble heart prompted them to adopt this stance. The word used for them is also extremely contemptuous: they are described as baggage that was left behind. These were people who, forsaking the Messenger of Allah, chose peace, tranquillity, and luxury in its place. They left the Messenger of Allah and the mujahidin alone, abandoning them to the hardships of the most intense heat, and they did not like to strive in the way of Allah with their lives and their wealth. They said, "Do not go out in this scorching heat." These are the very words that come from the mouths of all those who are fond of luxury. They are people of low resolve with the gait of women, and under no circumstances can they be called men.

These people are an example of feebleness of will. They are people of weak determination. In the world there are many who shrink from difficulties, hate struggle, and prefer humiliating comfort to the hardship of striving, and an honourable life of effort is not acceptable to them. They are accustomed to the life of the jackal rather than the life of the lion. Such people lie exhausted behind the lines that advance. But the forward ranks of the courageous cut through dangerous and thorny paths and move ahead. Therefore their nature is alive, and they know that confronting difficulties and continually moving forward is the demand of human nature. Compared with staying behind and sitting in houses, such people find more pleasure in facing the enemy.

Those who stayed behind rejoiced in their sitting [at home] in opposition to the Messenger of Allah, and they disliked striving with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah. And they said, "Do not go forth in this heat." Say: "The fire of Hell is more intense in heat," if only they understood.

In this world they will escape the heat by sheltering in the shade, but what remedy will they find for the heat of the Hereafter? There they will remain in the Fire forever. This is a realistic taunt from Allah. In this world, striving in the way of Allah is hardship for a very short period, compared with the heat of Hell, where whoever enters will remain for a long time, and it is known how long one will remain there.

Here, if anyone laughs, his laughter will be brief, because the life of this world is limited. And in the Hereafter he will then have to weep forever. And as he does, so he will be recompensed. This is an extremely just recompense.

These are the people who chose ease and adopted it in preference to jihad, and who, in difficult circumstances, remained behind the caravan of Islam. They have proved themselves incapable of any difficult undertaking. They are no longer fit for jihad. Therefore, no kind of leniency toward them is appropriate. Consequently, on no occasion should they be made to participate in jihad and be honoured, for on this important occasion they themselves spurned that honour.

The call to Islam and Islamic movements need people who are very strong, very sound of nature, and very upright, whose resolve is firm, who are able to overcome difficulties, who stand as a shield before the enemy, and who are prepared for a long and laborious struggle. But when people fond of luxury, seekers of ease, and people of weak conviction infiltrate the ranks of Islamic movements, they become the cause of its defeat at a difficult time. At a difficult time, they become the cause of agitation and disorder. Therefore, such people, from whom weakness and feebleness proceed during the course of a movement, should be cast away from the movement, so that in difficult times they do not become the cause of weakness and disorder, and so that it does not happen that when the age of prosperity arrives, when the age of conquest and success arrives, they return and enjoy its benefits. Say plainly: you will never walk with me now, nor can you fight alongside me against any enemy. You yourselves preferred to sit back the first time.

إنكم رضيتم بالقعود أول مرة (Innakum radītum bil-qu'ūd awwala marrah): "You were pleased with sitting back the first time." You have lost the honour of setting out for the Tabuk expedition. Since this honour could be attained only by one who was qualified for it, you have been deprived of the honour of joining the army of Tabuk. Therefore, no leniency can be shown to you in this matter, and you no longer deserve kind treatment or forgiveness. So now, sit with those who are your kind, your companions, and of your own disposition: فاقعدوا مع الخالفين (Fa'qu'udū ma'al-khālifīn), "So sit with those who stay behind." This was the path that Allah prescribed for His Prophet, and today too, the call and movement that is established following the footsteps of the Prophet will have this same way and course. Therefore, both the callers and the workers of the movement for Islam must keep this point in mind, in every age and in every place.

Just as the Messenger (ﷺ) was also commanded not to readmit these people into the Muslim ranks, because they abandoned him in difficult circumstances, in the same way this command was also given: that in future they should not be granted any honour or distinction in the Islamic society.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 84:

Regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, the exegetes have mentioned specific incidents, but the meaning of the verse is broader than those incidents. Here a principle is laid down concerning the group that struggles for the path of the Islamic way of life. Those who, in this struggle, are fond of luxury and comfort, who do not bear hardships and do not take part in difficult undertakings, should not be shown leniency by the Islamic leadership, nor should such people be given honour. Such people should be kept away from the Islamic ranks, or placed in the very last rows, and no leniency, kindness or tolerance should be shown to them in this matter.

What is stated in this verse is that their funeral prayer should not be offered and that you should not stand at their grave, because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they were disobedient, rebellious and hypocrites. But the general principle that emerges from this ruling is broader. For the funeral prayer and standing at the grave confer honour upon the deceased, and these people are not deserving of that honour. Especially those who do not stand in the ranks of the mujahidin at the most difficult time should not be given honour, so that people may come to know the importance of the Islamic struggle, and workers may know that in this matter those who deserve honour are only those who strive practically, who bear hardships, and who remain steadfast in difficulties. Only then will they become respected, honoured and distinguished in the Islamic ranks. In the Islamic movement, such people should be given neither outward honour nor inward honour.

The movement to establish the religion has this comprehensive guidance: no one should be honored because of their wealth and riches. Nor should any impression be taken from such people into the heart or the mind. These riches will themselves become a torment to them, for if anyone is impressed by their outward wealth, that too will be an honor for them. Within the heart, too, no awareness of esteeming such people should be allowed to arise. They should be completely disregarded.

Here two temperaments are described. One is the temperament of hypocrisy (nifaq), weakness and humiliation, and the other is the temperament of faith, which is strong and tested. The planning of the first temperament runs along the lines of cunning, staying behind, and accepting disgrace, while the planning of the second is directed toward steadfastness, spending, and the attainment of honour and dignity.

When a surah is revealed and it contains a command to jihad, some people who have the means, who possess adequate resources for the expenses of jihad, do not advance according to their position. Thus they do not give thanks for the blessings of Allah; rather, these people adopt the course of humiliation and shame. These people prefer to sit with women and the disabled. These people do not defend their own honour and their own standing. Such people are not even aware of this, nor do they realise how contemptible and abased they are becoming because of this course of theirs. Therefore they wish only to remain alive at any cost. Do they not understand that remaining alive at any cost is the work of the lowly?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verses 87–89:

﴿They are pleased to be with those who stayed behind (the women), and a seal has been set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾ ... ﴿That is the great success.﴾ ... If they understood, they would have grasped this truth: that in jihad lie strength, honour and a dignified life, and that in holding back from jihad lies weakness, humiliation, and a humiliating death.

It should be remembered that humiliation also has a price to be paid, and honour and dignity also require a person to pay a price. But sometimes a person pays a great price for humiliation in preference to honour. Some people of weak temperament think that honour requires a very great price, and that they cannot pay such a price. Therefore these people choose a life of disgrace, and when they see hardships and trials they run away. Such people live an utterly base, contemptible and frightful life. They fear their own shadow; they tremble at their own voice. They think every sound is aimed at them. The sign of such people is that life is very dear to them. Yet these people pay a higher price for that humiliation than for honour: the full price of their lives, the price of their dignity and self-respect, the price of their reputation, the price of their peace of mind, and the price of fear and of wealth. But these wretched people are not aware of it. Among such people were those who remained sitting with the women in Madinah; their hearts were sealed and their power of understanding ceased to function.

But the Messenger and those who believed with him were of a different kind. ﴿They strove with their wealth and their lives﴾ (Jahadu bi-amwalihim wa anfusihim). They fulfilled the demands of faith, paid the price of their convictions, and attained the honour that those who sat at home could not attain. These are the noble ones of this earth. In this world and the next, all treasures lie open before them, and their name and fame extend far and wide. These are the ones who will succeed: in this world, while they live a dignified life, and in the next, for whom Allah has prepared gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. This is the great success.
