They said: "Shall we remain in the cool shade with the women, while the other Muslims accompanying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) take part in the jihad? (This is a great sin.) By Allah! We will tie ourselves to the pillars, and will not untie ourselves until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself unties us." So they did just that. Three men remained who had not tied themselves up (al-Hadith).

Abd has transmitted the statement of Qatadah that this verse was revealed concerning seven men, of whom four, namely Abu Lubabah, Mirdas, Aws and Judham, had tied themselves to the pillars.

Ibn Mandah in al-Sahabah, and Abu al-Shaykh through the chain of Thawri from A'mash from Abu Sufyan, have transmitted the account of Hadrat Jabir that those who had been left behind from the company of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were: Abu Lubabah, Aws ibn Judham, Tha'labah ibn Wadi'ah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah. Abu Lubabah, Tha'labah (and others) had tied themselves to the pillars and (after their release) brought their wealth and presented it in the august presence, saying: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Accept it, for it was this that prevented us from accompanying you." The Messenger (ﷺ) said concerning these very men: "I will not untie them until Allah unties them." Concerning them the verse "And others who have acknowledged their sins..." was revealed. The chain of this hadith is strong.

Al-Baghawi has written: all the narrations agree on the name of Hadrat Abu Lubabah. Some people even think that the verse was revealed solely concerning Abu Lubabah.

Al-Baghawi has written: there is a difference as to what was the offence of Abu Lubabah for which this verse was revealed. Mujahid said: Abu Lubabah told the Banu Qurayzah that if they came down from their fortress agreeing to the judgment of (Sa'd ibn Mu'adh) they would be slaughtered (he indicated with his finger across his throat, meaning: it will happen, that is, you will be slaughtered). We have mentioned this story under the commentary of the verse of Surah al-Anfal, "O you who believe, do not betray Allah..." Ibn Ishaq and al-Bayhaqi also hold that Abu Lubabah's tying himself to the pillar was related to the incident of Banu Qurayzah.

Zuhri said that the revelation of the verse is connected with the incident of Tabuk. I say: perhaps Abu Lubabah tied himself to the pillar because of both faults. This is supported by the statements of Hadrat Ibn Abbas and Hadrat Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib mentioned above. Ibn Mardawayh, through the chain that includes Waqidi, has transmitted the account of Hadrat Umm Salamah that the verse concerning the acceptance of Abu Lubabah's repentance was revealed in my house. At dawn I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughing, so I said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! What is the reason for the laughter?" He said: "Abu Lubabah's repentance has been accepted." I said: "Shall I inform him of it?" He said: "As you wish." I stood at the door of the chamber and called out: "Abu Lubabah! Good news for you, Allah has accepted your repentance." This was before the command of the veil was revealed. Upon hearing the voice, people got up to untie Abu Lubabah. Abu Lubabah said: "(Not yet), let the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) come; only he will untie me." When in the morning the Messenger (ﷺ) came out of the house, he went and untied him, and the verse "And others who have acknowledged their sins..." was revealed.

From the hadith of Umm Salamah it is established that the fault whose forgiveness was revealed was the same fault that had occurred from Abu Lubabah concerning the Banu Qurayzah, because the expedition of Tabuk took place after the verse of the veil was revealed. Therefore, the preferable view is that the incident of tying to the pillar should be taken as the result of both stories, since both narrations are authentic.

﴿And pray for them﴾. Al-Baghawi has written: when taking the alms, is it obligatory upon the imam to supplicate for the giver? Some scholars hold it obligatory, others recommended. Some say that when receiving obligatory zakah, supplicating is obligatory, and when receiving voluntary charity, it is recommended. Some say that it is obligatory upon the imam, but if a poor person receives from a wealthy person, it is recommended for the giver to be prayed for.

Bukhari reports that Hadrat Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa said (Abu Awfa was among those who gave the pledge of renewal under the tree at Hudaybiyyah at the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)) that when people presented their charity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would (supplicate and) say: "O Allah! Send Your mercy upon them." So when my father presented his charity, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "O Allah! Send Your mercy upon the family of Abi Awfa."

The author of al-Qamus has written that in the language salah means: supplication, mercy, forgiveness, and the praise of the Messenger (ﷺ) by Allah. When the word salah is attributed to servants, it means supplication and forgiveness. This is the meaning intended in the verse. A hadith comes in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that if someone invites you to a meal, one should accept the invitation (and go). Then, if one is not fasting, one should eat; and if one is fasting, one should make salah, that is, supplicate for the host. Narrated by Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah.

Hadrat Jabir narrates that a woman said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Make salah for my husband," that is, pray for his forgiveness. The Messenger (ﷺ) prayed for him. Narrated by Ahmad. Ibn Hibban has authenticated this narration. When the word salah is attributed to Allah, it expresses mercy and approval. The supplication that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made for Abu Awfa, the salah in it means only mercy. Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i have narrated through Hadrat Qays ibn Sa'd that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah! Send Your salah and mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn Ubadah." The chain of this narration is excellent.

A marfu' narration from Hadrat Abu Hurayrah states that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that the angels say to the soul of the believer: "May Allah's mercy be upon you and upon your body."

In light of the words of the aforementioned hadiths and the linguistic meaning, Yahya ibn Yahya said that if the word salah is used for others besides the prophets, that is, if prayer is made for them using the word salah, there is no harm. However, it is a terminology of the muhaddithun and the fuqaha of Islam that the word salah is specific to the prophets, or is especially for our Prophet (ﷺ), and its use for others may be made only incidentally. Based on this terminology, Imam Malik said: "In my opinion, the use of the word salah for anyone other than the prophets is disliked." Qadi Iyad said that this statement is of Imam Malik and Sufyan, and this is also the view of the mutakallimun and the fuqaha. The fuqaha of Islam said: for others besides the prophets, words such as forgiveness, mercy and similar should be used (the word salah should not be used). The use of the word salah for others besides the prophets was not known (in the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the Umayyads); it was introduced in the era of the Banu Hashim, that is, the Abbasid caliphs (so it is an innovation).

Imam Abu Hanifah and a group of scholars said that the use of the word salah for others besides the prophets is not permissible on its own (that is, exclusively for non-prophets), but it is permissible incidentally (that is, if others are mentioned after the prophets, by way of following). This is because, in the terminology of the people of the Shariah, the word salah has been specialized to express the greatness of the prophets, especially the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so its use for others besides the prophets is not permissible. Allah said: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of one another to one another﴾. Based on this, Hadrat Ibn Abbas said: it is not appropriate to send salah upon anyone other than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (that is, to pray for someone using the word salah). Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah through the chain of Uthman ibn Hakim from Ikrimah, and this chain is sound.

Al-Bayhaqi said: the meaning of Hadrat Ibn Abbas's statement is that, as a mark of reverence, the word salah should not be mentioned for anyone other than the prophets; if it is in the sense of supplication, there is no harm. Ibn al-Qayyim said: the preferable view is that the word salah may be used generally, without any specific individual being named, for the prophets, angels, the Mothers of the Believers, the family of the Messenger, the descendants of the Messenger, and all people of obedience; and its use for a specific person other than the prophets is disliked. If it is used for a specific person, it will become a symbol (of a sect). Especially, the dislike increases when this word is used specifically for persons while other individuals who have virtues equal to, or even superior to, them are not given the word salah, and it is given to others, as the Rafidah do. Thus said Hafiz Ibn Hajar.

﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. Hadrat Ibn Abbas translated sakan as mercy. Abu Ubaydah translated it as composure of heart and tranquility of the soul, meaning that your prayer is a means of composure of the heart and the settling of the soul for them. They will be assured that Allah has accepted their repentance.

I say: when those with pure inner selves and clean hearts commit some sin, the darkness of sin overshadows their hearts and they begin to feel some gloom inside. But when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) makes supplication of forgiveness for them and Allah forgives them, the darkness and suffocation of the heart are removed. Or, the darkness and suffocation of sin within the heart are like the palpitation that arises when vapours rise from the stomach and gather around the sides of the heart, pressing on it; and when the pressure of the vapours is removed by correcting the stomach, the palpitation goes away. The same is the condition of the restlessness of the heart caused by the darkness arising from sin, and by forgiveness it is removed and composure and tranquility are produced. Truly has it been said: by the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾, of their acknowledgment of fault and of the supplication and forgiveness-seeking of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for them.

﴿All-Knowing﴾, well aware of their remorse (and repentance).

Al-Baghawi (regarding the occasion of revelation of the following verse) has written: when the repentance of these people was accepted, those who had remained behind (out of laziness or some other reason) from Tabuk and had not repented (by openly confessing their sin), said: "Yesterday these people were with us, no one associated with them, nor did anyone speak with them. Now what new matter has occurred?" Upon this, the following verse was revealed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 104:

Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity? Does it not know that Allah Himself accepts the repentance of His servants and takes (receives) their charities with the hand of acceptance? That is, He accepts them in the way that someone takes a thing to give in return as compensation.

It is narrated from Hazrat Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul! When a servant gives charity from lawful earnings, and Allah accepts only what is pure, and only what is pure (speech, deed, charity) ascends to the heavens, then it is as if he places that charity in the hand of Allah, and Allah nurtures it for him in His hand, just as you nurture your young one (by passing your hand over its back again and again), until a morsel becomes as large as a great mountain on the Day of Resurrection." After saying this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the verse: "Indeed, Allah is He who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charities." Narrated by al-Shafi'i.

The narration in the Sahihain is similar in meaning to this narration; it adds that whoever gives a charity equal to a date from lawful earnings, and Allah accepts only what is pure, then Allah accepts it with His right hand, etc.

"And indeed Allah is the Accepter of repentance, the Most Merciful." That is, accepting the repentance of those who repent and showing mercy to them is His attribute.

And say (to them): This address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to all people.

Do (whatever you wish) to act.

Then Allah will see your deeds; nothing of them is hidden from Him.

And His Messenger and the believers (will also see). Whatever you conceal, Allah will disclose it to His Messenger through revelation, and then the believers too will come to know of it.

Mujahid said: This is a warning. The meaning of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeing is that Allah will inform His Prophet, and the believers' knowledge will come about in this way: Allah will place in their hearts love for the righteous, and He will place in the hearts of the people of faith aversion toward those who are corrupt.

And you will be returned to the One who knows the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do. And surely you will be brought to Him who knows all that is open and hidden, and so He will tell you all that you did.

﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command, [for] He may punish them or He may accept their repentance.﴾ That is, among the people of Madinah, those who did not go out on the expedition to Tabuk, there are others whose case remains suspended until Allah's command arrives: He may punish them if He wills, and He has the authority to punish even for a minor sin (saghirah), or He may forgive them without repentance if He wills, and He can forgive major sins (kabirah) without repentance. Nothing is binding upon Him. Therefore, servants should both hope and remain fearful. (For Allah there is no hesitation at all in punishing or forgiving anyone; His knowledge is certain as to whom He will forgive and whom He will punish. Doubt exists in the knowledge of servants, and hesitation regarding punishment and forgiveness is only fitting for servants. Therefore, in the verse, the word ﴿imma﴾ ("either... or") is used in relation to the servants. That is, ﴿imma﴾ is used at the occasion of doubt and hesitation, and servants may be uncertain about forgiveness and punishment, so the word ﴿imma﴾ is mentioned in keeping with their knowledge.)

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ And Allah knows well their condition, and He is also aware of the wisdom behind the treatment He will give them. Al-Bukhari and Muslim have narrated, through the report of Ka'b ibn Malik, a lengthy hadith (a narration from the Prophet ﷺ) which shows that by ﴿and others are deferred until Allah's command﴾ are meant Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah and Murarah ibn al-Rabi'. These were among the ten men who did not take part in Tabuk, and they had not tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque (as others had). However, they openly confessed their fault and made no excuse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had commanded the Muslims that they should cut off greetings and conversation with these three. When these men saw this treatment, they repented with sincerity of intention and entrusted their matter to Allah. Finally, Allah showed mercy to them (and their fault was also pardoned). We will write their story further on.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated it through the report of Abu Rahm Kulthum ibn Husayn al-Ghifari. Abu Rahm was among those who had given the bai'ah (pledge of allegiance; a renewal of allegiance) at Hudaybiyyah under the tree at the hand of the Messenger ﷺ.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi, in his Dala'il, narrated through the report of Ibn 'Abbas. Also, Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through the report of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Muhammad ibn 'Umar narrated through Yazid ibn Ruman, that the clan of 'Amr ibn 'Awf built a mosque and sent a man to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asking him to come and pray in that mosque. When the clan of Ghanm ibn 'Awf saw this, they felt envy and said: "We too will build a mosque like the one they have built." (The matter was this: before departing for Syria, Abu 'Amir al-Fasiq had told them: "Build a mosque and gather as many weapons as possible in it (secretly). I am going to the Caesar of Rome, and from there I will bring a Roman army and expel Muhammad ﷺ and his companions from here.") Abu 'Amir al-Fasiq had gone out from Madinah with the intention of rebelling against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and fighting the Messenger ﷺ. So these people were waiting for the arrival of Abu 'Amir (and the bringing of the Roman army). When the mosque was ready, they wished that the Messenger ﷺ would pray in it, so that their purpose, namely mischief, disbelief and enmity towards Islam, might find an opportunity to succeed. When the Messenger ﷺ was preparing to set out for Tabuk, some of them came into his presence and said: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ! We have built a mosque. Its purpose is that those who are sick or in need, who cannot come to the blessed mosque, or on a very cold night, or on a rainy night when people cannot come from there to here, may pray in this mosque. We wish that you would come and pray in this mosque." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Now I am on a journey and occupied with my tasks. When we return, God willing, we will pray in your mosque." So when he returned from Tabuk and stopped at the place Dhu Awan, the following verse was revealed. This place was at a distance of one hour's journey from Madinah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 107:

﴿And those who took a mosque by way of harm﴾ — and there are some people who built a mosque with the intention of causing harm (to Islam), that is, to cause harm to the Muslims. Ibn Ishaq has written that twelve men took part in the construction of this mosque: (1) Hizam bin Khalid of the Bani Ubayd bin Zayd clan, who was a member of Bani Amr bin Awf; (2) Thalabah bin Hatib of the Bani Umayyah bin Zayd clan; (3) Mu'attib bin Qushayr of the Bani Subay'ah bin Zayd clan; (4) Habibah bin Azar; (5) Nabtal bin Harith; (6) Najjad bin Uthman; (7) Abbad bin Hanif of the Bani Amr bin Awf clan, who was the brother of Sahl bin Hanif; (8) Harithah bin Amir and his two sons; (9) Majma' bin Harithah; (10) Zayd bin Harithah; (11) Wadi'ah bin Thabit; and another person called (12) Bakhraj. All of them took part in building this mosque in order to cause harm to the Masjid of Quba.

﴿And disbelief﴾ — because of their denial of Allah and His Messenger.

﴿And to cause division among the believers﴾ — to create discord among the Muslims. The Muslims used to pray in the Masjid of Quba, and Majma' bin Harithah used to pray there. These people built the second mosque for the purpose that some of those who prayed in the Masjid of Quba would begin to pray in this mosque, and thus (in the name of religion) the Muslims would be divided into factions and disagreement would arise.

﴿And as a station for him who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before﴾ — and to provide a base for the person who was already an opponent of Allah and His Messenger.

Baghawi has written: "Him who had warred against Allah" refers to Abu Amir the monk, who was the father of Hanzalah Ghasil al-Malaikah and a member of the Bani Amr bin Awf clan. Before Islam, this man had become a Christian monk wearing a woollen cloak. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu Amir asked: "What religion is this that you have brought?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is the pure religion of Tawhid, which was the religion of Ibrahim." Abu Amir said: "I am already upon the Hanifiyyah religion." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are not upon the Hanifiyyah (the religion of Ibrahim)." Abu Amir said: "Why not? (Certainly I am upon the religion of Ibrahim.) You have added other things into the Hanifiyyah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have not done so; I have brought the pure, clear and luminous Shariah." Abu Amir said: "Whichever of us is a liar, may Allah cause him to die alone, estranged from his home, while travelling." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah do so." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him Abu Amir the Fasiq (instead of the monk). On the day of the Battle of Uhud, Abu Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whatever people fight you, I will join them and fight you." Accordingly, until the Battle of Hunayn, he continued to fight against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alongside other peoples. After the defeat of Hawazin, he fled to Syria, and a message was sent to the hypocrites: "Be ready. Build a mosque and keep in it as many weapons as you can. I am going to the Caesar of Rome, and from there I will bring a Roman army and expel Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions." On Abu Amir's advice, these people built a mosque alongside the Masjid of Quba.

Here, "min qablu" may mean either: that before building the mosque, this person had already rebelled and waged war against Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ); or that it means they had already built the mosque before the absence from the Tabuk expedition. In the first meaning, "min qablu" is connected with "harab", and in the second case it is connected with "ittakhadhu".

﴿And they will swear: "We intended nothing but good."﴾ — and these people will swear that they had no intention other than good.

﴿Al-Husna﴾ — good, that is, comfort for the Muslims in intense heat and rain, and facilitation for the weak and infirm who could not reach the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was what we had in view. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, through the chain of Awfi, have related the statement of Ibn Abbas that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had the Masjid of Quba built, some Ansar, among whom was a man named Bakhraj, went and built the "mosque of hypocrisy." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Bakhraj: "What is your purpose in this?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), my purpose is only good." Upon this, this verse was revealed.

﴿And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.﴾ — and Allah is witness that these people are liars in their word and their oath.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 108:

Lā taqum fīhi abadan: "Do not ever stand [for prayer] in it." Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿAbbās (RA) also gave this as the explanation.

Ibn al-Najjār said: The hypocrites built this mosque in opposition to the Mosque of Qubā. They all used to gather there, speak ill of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and mock him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the place called Dhī Awān on his return from Tabūk, this verse was revealed.

Ibn Isḥāq, through al-Zuhrī, narrated from Ḥaḍrat Abū Rahm that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Mālik ibn Dukhshum of the Banū Sālim ibn ʿAwf and Maʿn ibn ʿAdī of the clan of ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī. Baghawī mentioned ʿĀmir ibn Iskan and Waḥshī, the slayer of Ḥaḍrat Ḥamzah, along with Mālik ibn Dukhshum; he did not mention ʿĀṣim. Dhahabī, in al-Tajrīd, also named Suwayd ibn ʿAbbās al-Anṣārī and said: "Go and demolish and burn this mosque built by people who are ungrateful to the truth." On the command, these men went off quickly, and on reaching the locality of Sālim ibn ʿAwf, Mālik said to his two companions: "Wait for me, I will come." Saying this, he went to his house, took some dry palm branches, set them alight, and then all these men ran and reached the mosque between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ; at that time the people of the mosque were present in it. These men set fire to the mosque and demolished it, leveling it with the ground. The people of the mosque scattered in different directions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered: "Make this place a rubbish dump where people, animals, and filth are thrown." Abū ʿĀmir the wicked died alone in the land of Shām, ruined and in a state of travel.

Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf al-Ṣāliḥī states that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madīnah, he offered ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī the place of this mosque so that he might build his house there. Ḥaḍrat ʿĀṣim said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! After the command Allah has revealed concerning this mosque, I cannot build a house in it. However, grant this place to Thābit ibn Aqram, as he has no house." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted that place to Thābit, but no child was born to Thābit in that house; no pigeon hatched its young there, and no hen hatched its eggs there (i.e., no chick emerged by sitting on the eggs).

Baghawī said: It is related that the Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, who had built the Mosque of Qubā, came into the presence of Ḥaḍrat ʿUmar and requested that Majmaʿ ibn Ḥārithah be appointed imam in their mosque. Ḥaḍrat ʿUmar refused and said: "May his eye not be cooled; was he not the imam of the Mosque of Ḍirār?" Ḥaḍrat Majmaʿ said: "Commander of the Faithful! Do not be hasty in deciding against me. I did indeed pray in the Mosque of Ḍirār, but I did not know what those people's intention was. Had I known their hidden purpose, I would not have prayed there. I was a boy who had memorized the Qur'an, while they were old and unlettered, so I led the prayer. I thought their aim in building the mosque was to gain reward; I had no knowledge of the thoughts in their hearts." Ḥaḍrat ʿUmar accepted Ḥaḍrat Majmaʿ's excuse, confirmed his statement, and ordered him to lead the prayer in the Mosque of Qubā.

La-masjidun ussisa ʿala al-taqwā min awwali yawmin aḥaqqu an taqūma fīhi: "A mosque founded upon piety from the first day is more deserving that you stand [for prayer] in it." "From the first day" means the first day of its construction and foundation, or the first day of the Prophet's (ﷺ) settling in Madīnah after the Hijrah. Thus said al-Suhaylī. Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿUmar, Ḥaḍrat Zayd ibn Thābit, and Ḥaḍrat Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: "Masjidun" refers to the Prophet's Mosque, that is, the mosque in Madīnah. Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Tirmidhī, Nasāʾī, Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Bayhaqī (in al-Dalāʾil) have related that Ḥaḍrat Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said: I came into the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) at the house of one of the Mothers of the Believers and asked: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Which mosque is it (about which it is said) that its foundation was laid upon piety?" The Messenger (ﷺ) took a handful of pebbles, threw them on the ground, and said: "It is this mosque of yours, the mosque of Madīnah."

Ṭabarānī and Ḍiyāʾ al-Maqdisī in al-Mukhtārah related, through Ḥaḍrat Zayd ibn Thābit, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the mosque whose foundation was laid upon piety, and he said: "It is this mosque of mine."

Ibn Abī Shaybah and Ibn Mardawayh report that Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿUmar was asked: "Which mosque was founded upon piety?" He said: "The mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Regarding the virtue of the Prophet's Mosque, there is the hadith which Shaykhān (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) related in their Ṣaḥīḥ through Ḥaḍrat Abū Hurayrah: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between my house and my pulpit is one of the gardens of Paradise, and my pulpit is upon my Ḥawḍ (Pool)." (Or it may be translated thus: "Between my house and my pulpit there will be one of the gardens of Paradise, and my pulpit will be upon my Ḥawḍ. Wa Allāhu aʿlam.") In the narration of Baghawī, instead of "house," the word "grave" (qabr) occurs.

Shaykhān, Aḥmad and Nasāʾī related through Ḥaḍrat ʿAbdullāh ibn Zayd al-Māzinī that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise." Tirmidhī also related the same from Ḥaḍrat ʿAlī.

Ḥaḍrat Abū Hurayrah narrates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers in other mosques, except the Masjid al-Ḥarām (the Kaʿbah)."

Some scholars hold that the mosque "founded upon piety" is the Mosque of Qubā. This statement of Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿAbbās appears in the narration of ʿAṭiyyah. Ḥaḍrat ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Ḥaḍrat Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatādah also held this view. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) founded the Mosque of Qubā. When he came to Madīnah after migrating, he stayed in Qubā for as many days as from Monday to Friday, and prayed in it during that period. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Bayhaqī related this from Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿAbbās, and Abū al-Shaykh related it from Ḍaḥḥāk.

Bukhārī, through ʿAbdullāh ibn Dīnār, related Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿUmar's account that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to go to the Mosque of Qubā every Saturday, on foot or riding, and Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿUmar also did so. Nāfiʿ related the additional statement of Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray two rakʿahs in it. Dāwūdī, Suhaylī and Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar said: This is not a difference (of tafsir), because each of the two mosques was founded upon piety.

I say: The meaning is that although the occasion of revelation is specific, the consideration is the generality of the wording; "masjidun" is an indefinite noun described by "ussisa ʿala al-taqwā," and this description is also general. But the flow of the verse indicates that the Mosque of Qubā is intended, and the verse was revealed concerning it, because the building of the Mosque of Ḍirār was done precisely to harm the Mosque of Qubā. Then the following verse also confirms this, where it says:

Fīhi rijālun yuḥibbūna an yatatahharū wa-llāhu yuḥibbu al-muṭahhirīn: "In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves." "Purifying oneself" means being pure from impurity, major ritual impurity, filth (najāsah), sin, and bad character. Baghawī related with his chain from Ḥaḍrat Abū Hurayrah that the verse "Fīhi rijālun yuḥibbūna an yatatahharū" was revealed concerning the people of Qubā. They used to cleanse themselves with water after relieving themselves, so this verse was revealed concerning them. Tirmidhī has the same narration.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ḥaḍrat Ibn ʿAbbās that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out on foot with the Muhājirūn and, arriving at the door of the Mosque of Qubā, stood there. Inside, the Anṣār were sitting. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Are you believers?" The Anṣār remained silent. He repeated it, and then Ḥaḍrat ʿUmar said: "They are certainly believers, and I am with them." He said: "Are you content with Allah's decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you endure calamity patiently?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Do you give thanks in ease?" They said: "Yes." He said: "By the Lord of the Kaʿbah, you are believers." Then he sat down among them and said: "O group of Anṣār! Allah has praised you. What do you do at the time of wuḍūʾ and relieving yourselves?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! After relieving ourselves we use three stones, and after the stones we use water." Upon this, the Messenger (ﷺ) recited the verse "Fīhi rijālun yuḥibbūna an yatatahharū."

Ibn Khuzaymah in his Ṣaḥīḥ has written, through Ḥaḍrat ʿUwaymir ibn Sāʿidah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went to the people of Qubā in the Mosque of Qubā and said: "In the matter of your mosque, Allah has praised your purity very well. How do you perform purification?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! By Allah, we know nothing else; only this was the case: the Jews who lived in our neighborhood used to cleanse with water after relieving themselves, so we too began to cleanse with water." In another narration it is stated: "We use water after using stones." He said: "That is it; you should certainly continue doing so."

ʿUmar ibn Shabbah, in Akhbār al-Madīnah, related through Walīd ibn Abī al-Mundhir from Yaḥyā ibn Sahl al-Anṣārī that Ḥaḍrat Sahl al-Anṣārī said: This verse was revealed concerning the people of Qubā, who cleansed with water after relieving themselves.

Ibn Jarīr related the statement of ʿAṭāʾ that some people of Qubā invented purification with water. It was concerning them that the verse "Fīhi rijālun yuḥibbūna an yatatahharū" was revealed.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 109:

﴿Is one who founded his building on the fear of Allah and His pleasure better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling precipice, so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell?﴾ Here the question is rhetorical, and since the answer was clear, it has not been mentioned. "Bunyanahu" means the foundation of his religion or the foundation of his building. "Ala taqwa" means upon firm walls and foundations of the fear of Allah and the seeking of His pleasure. "Ala shafa jurufin" means upon the weakest foundations and the most feeble walls. Shafa, shafir and jurf all mean an edge, that is, the edge of a valley or watercourse which, owing to flooding, has been hollowed out inside, so that the tip of the edge juts outward. "Hara" means split and near to falling. The original form of "haar" is "hawir", and according to al-Baghawi it is "hā'ir". It has also been said that this word derives from "hāra yahāru", and "hāra" means it fell or collapsed. Here "hār" means an edge that is about to fall.

The meaning is this: whoever established his building upon firm foundations, that is, upon the fear of Allah and the seeking of His pleasure, is better; or whoever raised his building upon the weakest foundations, that is, upon falsehood and hypocrisy, is better? The opposite of taqwa is shirk and hypocrisy, so "shafa jurufin" is used metaphorically to mean shirk and hypocrisy. "Fanhara bihi": Hazrat Ibn Abbas said: their hypocrisy carried them into Hell. Al-Baghawi said: the meaning is that the building of this mosque, for the purpose of harm, is like one constructed on the far edge of Hell (its brink), which will collapse and drop those who built it above into Hell.

Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Salihi quoted the statement of Ibn Atiyyah. It is narrated that Hazrat Abdullah ibn Umar said: the mosque whose founding and foundation has been declared to be upon taqwa refers to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In "Afaman assasa bunyanahu ala taqwa min Allahi wa ridwan", "bunyan" refers to Masjid Quba. And in "Am man assasa bunyanahu ala shafa jurufin", "bunyan" refers, by consensus, to Masjid Dirar.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, that is, He does not show them the path of righteousness and salvation.

Ibn al-Mundhir quoted the statements of Hazrat Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and Juraij, and Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the report of Qatadah. All three of these scholars state: it was related to us that when a place was dug in the Masjid Dirar, people saw smoke rising from there. Al-Baghawi quoted the account of Hazrat Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: I saw smoke rising from Masjid Dirar.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 9, verse 110:

Lā yazāl bunyānahumu alladhī banaw rībatan fī qulūbihim: "The building which they have built will never cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts." Rībatan means doubt and hypocrisy, that is, this building will remain a cause of the growth of doubt and hypocrisy in their hearts, and they will continue to think that they did a good deed. This is like the love of the calf that took root in the hearts of the people of Musa (Moses). (In the same way, the love of this mosque of harm has become fixed in the hearts of these hypocrites.) Ibn Abbas gave this same interpretation. Kalbi translated rībatan as regret and remorse, because these people came to feel regret over the building of this mosque. Sudi interpreted rībatan as rage, meaning that the demolition of this building will always kindle anger and fury within their hearts.

Illā an tuqatta'a qulūbuhum: "Unless their hearts are torn to pieces" (then doubt will be removed from their hearts). That is, hypocrisy will remain constantly lodged in their hearts, but it will end only when their hearts themselves are torn apart and a time comes when there is no capacity left in their hearts to know. Some scholars said: the tearing of hearts into pieces means the killing of the hypocrites, or their going into the grave, or their entering Hell. Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said: they will remain in doubt until the moment of death; when they die, the doubt will be removed and they will have certainty of the truth.

Wallahu 'Alimun Hakim: "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." (He knows their intentions, and He is aware of the wisdom behind His command to tear down the mosque of harm.)

The biographers have related that in the eleventh year of the Prophethood, during the season of Hajj, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, that is, came out of Makkah, and presented his prophethood to the tribes of Arabia. One day, while he was near a mountain pass, he met a group from the tribe of Khazraj. The Messenger (ﷺ) asked: "Who are you?" They replied: "We are people of Khazraj." He said: "Could you sit for a while? I would like to speak with you." The Khazrajis replied: "Certainly." So they all sat down with the Messenger (ﷺ). He invited them to come to Allah, presented Islam to them, and recited the Qur'an to them.

It is the power of Allah that the Jews lived in those settlements alongside these people, and they were People of the Book. The Aws and Khazraj were more numerous than the Jews, but all of them were idol-worshippers. When there was some dispute between these people and the Jews, the Jews would say: "A prophet is about to be sent; the time of his coming is near. We will join him and kill you."

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with these people, they recognised his qualities (because they already had knowledge of the qualities of the coming Prophet from the statements of the Jews), and they said to one another: "Look! Do not let the Jews reach him before you do." So they all accepted the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) invitation, and six men of the tribe of Khazraj became Muslims: As'ad bin Zurarah, Awf bin Harith, whose mother's name was Afra, Rafi bin Malik, Qutbah bin Amir bin Jadidah, Uqbah bin Amir bin Nabi, and Jabir bin Abdullah bin Ribab. In some narrations, the name of Ubadah bin Samit appears in place of Jabir. Some have stated that seven men became Muslims, thus combining Jabir and Ubadah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Will you support me so that I may convey the message of my Lord?" They replied: "(O Messenger of Allah!) Only last year the battle of Bu'ath took place between us; on that day we shed much blood among ourselves. If you come to us in such a state, our whole group will not be able to stand with you. Now, please permit us to return to our tribes; perhaps Allah will reconcile us, and we will invite them to the same thing to which you have invited us. We hope that at that time Allah will unite everyone in supporting you, and if all become your followers, then no one will oppose you. We will meet you again next year at the time of Hajj." After this conversation, these gentlemen returned to Madinah, and after their return to Madinah, the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spread into every house of the Ansar; there was no house in which he was not mentioned. Then in the following year, that is, in the twelfth year of the Prophethood, twelve or eleven men came and met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the pass. This was the second pass. Of these twelve, five were those mentioned above besides Jabir, and seven were: Mu'adh bin Harith, the brother of Awf bin Harith, Dhakwan, Ubadah bin Samit, Yazid bin Thalabah, Abbas bin Ubadah bin Fadlah. These five were all from Khazraj, and two persons were from the tribe of Aws: Abu al-Haytham bin Taihan of Banu al-Ashhal, and Uwaymir bin Sa'idah.

(In Surah al-Mumtahanah) the pledge of women described there was the same covenant with which all of them pledged allegiance, that is, they said that they would not associate partners with Allah, would not steal, and so on. When all had become Muslims, they returned to Madinah. On reaching Madinah, As'ad bin Zurarah began gathering all those who continued to become Muslims in Madinah. The tribes of Aws and Khazraj sent a petition to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking that he send someone to them who would teach them the Qur'an. The Messenger (ﷺ) sent Mus'ab bin Umayr. At that time there were forty Muslims in Madinah; through Mus'ab's efforts many people became Muslims. Sa'd bin Mu'adh and Usayd bin Hudayr also became Muslims, and through the conversion of these two elders, all the men and women of Banu Abd al-Ashhal became Muslims. Then in the thirteenth year of the Prophethood, at the third pass, during the days of Tashriq, the people of Madinah came, and seventy or seventy-three men and two women pledged allegiance. Al-Hakim stated that they were seventy-five persons.

Ibn Jarir, on the authority of Muhammad bin Ka'b al-Qurazi, and also Baghawi, mentioned that Abdullah bin Rawahah said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Take from us whatever conditions you wish, for your Lord and for yourself." The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Regarding my Lord, I stipulate that you worship Him and not associate anything with Him (that is, not worship anything else); and for myself, I stipulate that you protect me with the same protection with which you protect your own lives and wealth (that is, protect me as you protect your own selves and property)." The Ansar said: "If we do this, what will we get?" He said: "Paradise." The Ansar said: "This is a profitable bargain; we will neither cancel this bargain nor allow it to be cancelled (or we will not wish to cancel it)." Then the following verse was revealed:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for that they will have Paradise.﴾ Allah has made the granting of Paradise in return for the expenditure of life and wealth a matter of buying and selling.

The historians (ahl al-sair) have written that the first person to place his hand in the blessed hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Bara' ibn Ma'rur, or Abu al-Haytham, or As'ad, and that they made the condition that from whatever calamity they protected their families and dependents, they would also protect the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and would support him against every white and black (that is, against all of mankind). The first verse revealed concerning fighting and jihad was this verse; after it came ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against...﴾ etc.

When the pledge of the night of the defile (al-'Aqabah) was concluded, and this pledge had been taken secretly from the Quraysh of Makkah, the Messenger of Allah then ordered his companions to leave Makkah and migrate to Madinah, while he himself remained in Makkah awaiting permission (from Allah).

One year before the pledge of the third 'Aqabah, Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Asad, who had come from Abyssinia and whom the people of Makkah had caused great hardship, upon receiving news that the Ansar had become Muslim, migrated to Madinah. He was the first among the Madinan emigrants. Then Amir ibn Rabi'ah and his wife Layla emigrated, then 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh, then other Muslims one after another, then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and his brother Zayd, and 'Abbas ibn Rabi'ah with twenty riders. All of them, upon reaching Madinah, camped in the outskirts of Madinah. Then 'Uthman ibn 'Affan emigrated. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq repeatedly requested the Messenger (ﷺ) for permission to migrate, but the Messenger (ﷺ) kept saying: "Do not be hasty, perhaps Allah will make a companion for you." The thought was that perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would also migrate along with them. After that, the Quraysh gathered in the assembly hall (and secretly plotted to martyr the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)). The plot of the Quraysh and the migration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have been described in Surah al-Anfal, which indicates that this verse is Makki.

﴿They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed.﴾ This is an introductory statement, in which the purpose of the purchase is expressed. Some exegetes said that yuqatiluna (although it is in the present tense form) carries the meaning of a command (i.e., fight, kill, and be killed).

﴿A true promise binding upon Him﴾: Allah has made a true and firm promise to give Paradise in return for this purchase. The pronoun in 'alayhi refers to the condition (al-shart), and wa'dan is a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq) for an omitted verb, for emphasis. Haqqan is either an adjective of wa'dan, or it is also a maf'ul mutlaq of an omitted verb.

﴿In the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran﴾: The explicit mention of the promise in the Torah and the Gospel indicates that the Jews and Christians were also commanded to wage jihad, and were promised Paradise in return.

﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ (This is a rhetorical interrogative of denial.)

That is, there is no one. Breaking a promise is evil, and its occurrence from Allah is impossible. Fulfilling a promise is generosity, and there is no one more generous than Allah. By mentioning the negation in interrogative form, the faithfulness to the covenant is expressed with emphasis, and the truth of Allah's promise is made clear through emphatic style of speech.

﴿So rejoice in your transaction which you have concluded﴾: So rejoice greatly and celebrate. This is an address to the believers who fight in jihad. Earlier their mention was in the third person; now they are addressed directly. The reason for the good news is that by giving up a perishable, worthless thing, they have obtained an everlasting, sublime blessing. What could be a more profitable bargain than this?

'Umar said: Allah bought from you and made the profit of both transactions for your sake. Qatadah said: Allah gave them a price, and a very great one. Hasan said: Listen to the message of a profitable trade, in which Allah has bought from every believer and benefited him. This is also the saying of Hasan al-Basri: Allah gave you the world, so with some of the world buy Paradise.

﴿And that is the great success﴾: And this (sale) is indeed the great achievement, the attainment of which is the ultimate goal.

**Al-Ta'ibun** (those who repent from polytheism), that is, those who have repented of shirk and become free of hypocrisy.

*Al-ta'ibun* is the predicate (khabar), with an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: they are those who repent. That is, those who have pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and taken on the obligation to carry out all the commands are possessed of all the qualities mentioned in this verse. It is also possible that *al-ta'ibun* is the subject (mubtada') and the qualities mentioned afterwards are the predicate, meaning: in reality, those who possess these qualities are the ones who [truly] repent. It is also possible that the predicate is omitted, meaning: those who repent are people of Paradise, even if they did not take part in jihad at that time, provided that there is no feeling of enmity and hostility in them and no intention that, when Allah grants them the strength for jihad, they will still not perform jihad. Zajjaj said: it is as if (in this case) the promise of Paradise is for all believers, as Allah said in another verse: *"And to each Allah has promised the good (reward)"* — and Allah has promised good to all.

**Al-'abidun** (those who worship [Allah alone], abandoning both overt and covert shirk), those who worship.

**Al-hamidun** (those who praise [Allah] in both ease and hardship), those who praise. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The ones who praise Allah abundantly, who praise Him in both ease and hardship (that is, in every state, whether comfort or affliction), will be called first to Paradise. Narrated by al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, with a sahih chain, from Ibn 'Abbas.

**Al-sa'ihun** (those who fast). Ibn Jarir has recorded, through the narration of Hadrat 'Ubayd ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked the meaning of *al-sa'ihun*. He said: those who fast. Baghawi has also reported this same statement from Hadrat Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Mardawayh has transmitted a mawquf statement from Hadrat 'A'ishah that in this verse, *siyahah* (touring) means fasting.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: The fasting person is called a *sa'ih* because he abandons all pleasures, eating, drinking, and marital intimacy (just as a traveler is deprived of those pleasures). Hadrat Abu Hurayrah narrates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The reward of every good deed of the children of Adam is multiplied from ten times to seven hundred times, except fasting, concerning which Allah has said that fasting is for Me and I alone will reward it. The servant gives up his desire and food for My sake (the hadith…). Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh).

'Ata' said: *al-sa'ihun* refers to the ghazis who fight in the way of Allah. As Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have narrated with a sahih chain from Hadrat Abu Umamah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The *siyahah* of my ummah is jihad in the way of Allah. Baghawi has written: It is narrated that Hadrat 'Uthman ibn Maz'un said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), permit me to travel (for *siyahah*)." He said: "The *siyahah* of my ummah is jihad in the way of Allah."

'Ikrimah said: Those who travel for *siyahah* are students of knowledge who wander through lands in pursuit of knowledge. Hadrat Abu al-Darda' states: I myself heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Whoever treads a path in search of knowledge, Allah will make him tread the path to Paradise, and the angels lay down their wings for the seeker of knowledge, and they seek forgiveness for the scholar, those (angels) who are in the heavens and those (angels and humans and jinn) who are on the earth, and the fish in the water. The superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like the superiority of the full moon on the fourteenth night over the other stars. The scholars are the heirs of the prophets; the prophets did not leave dinars or dirhams as inheritance, but left knowledge as inheritance. Whoever takes it has taken an abundant share. Narrated by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Abu Dawud.

**Al-raki'un al-sajidun** (those who bow and prostrate), that is, those who perform prayer. The mention of those who pray with two words, *al-raki'un al-sajidun* — both refer to those who pray — (so it is as if the praying ones are mentioned twice). The repetition of the mention indicates that prayer has precedence over all other acts of worship. Hadrat Ibn Mas'ud states that I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which deed is most beloved to Allah?" He said: "Prayer at its proper time." I said: "What after that?" He said: "Obedience to one's parents." I said: "What after that?" He said: "Jihad in the way of Allah." Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim. Abu Nu'aym narrated through the narration of Fadl ibn Dukayn that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Prayer is the pillar of the religion.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated through Hadrat Anas that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: Prayer is the light of the believer. Qada'i narrated through Hadrat 'Ali that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: For every person of piety, prayer is a means of nearness (to Allah). Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated through Hadrat Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: In prostration the servant is closest to his Lord more than in any other state, so make abundant supplication.

**Al-amirun bil-ma'ruf** (those who enjoin good), that is, those who enjoin faith and obedience.

**Wal-nahun 'an al-munkar** (and those who forbid evil), that is, those who forbid shirk and sin. Some scholars said: *al-ma'ruf* means the Sunnah and *al-munkar* means innovation (bid'ah). Mentioning the conjunction (wa, "and") between the two indicates that these two qualities together constitute one single characteristic.

**Wal-hafizun li-hudud Allah** (and those who observe the limits of Allah), that is, those who safeguard the ordinances and laws which Allah has established between the servant and Allah.

Some scholars have written that by mentioning *al-hafizun* separately with the conjunction (wa), attention is drawn to the fact that the excellent qualities mentioned earlier in detail are summarized in the observance of the limits of Allah. The former was detail, this is summary.

I say: Perhaps this is also the reason: the praiseworthy qualities mentioned in the preceding speech are bounded in this phrase, so that nothing is added to them from one's own side, neither monasticism, nor is anything reduced from outward form or inward meaning. Thus, the sum of the above qualities means the observance of the ordinances and the guarding of the limits, which means sincerity and complete attentiveness, since observing limits is not possible without complete inward attentiveness. And sincerity and attentiveness of heart are obtained through the company of hearts that are alive.

**Wa-bashshir al-mu'minin** (and give glad tidings to the believers), that is, give glad tidings to those in whom the qualities mentioned above exist. The word *al-mu'minin* indicates that faith demands the aforementioned qualities, and the complete believer is one who possesses those qualities.

The good news is not specified, because the blessing for which glad tidings are commanded is so magnificent that it cannot be described, nor can it be conceived in anyone's mind, nor has anyone heard of it. And Allah knows best.

Shaykhayn (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated in the Sahihayn through the narration of the father of Hadrat Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that when Abu Talib was dying, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him. He found Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah present there. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to Abu Talib: "Uncle, say 'La ilaha illa Allah' once, so that I may present it as evidence on your behalf before Allah." Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah said: "Abu Talib! Will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept presenting the word of Tawhid (again and again), while Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah kept repeating their words, until finally Abu Talib said: "On the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib." In another narration it is further added that when Abu Talib refused to say "La ilaha illa Allah," the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah! I will keep asking forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden." Then the following verse was revealed:

The Prophet and the believers are not permitted to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they are near kin, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire. (Qur'an 9:113)

This verse shows that it is permissible to pray for the forgiveness of living polytheists, because such a prayer means a request that the polytheists be granted the grace of faith (and there is no harm in this; rather, it is commendable). Muslim has related from Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his uncle: "Say: There is no god but Allah, and I will testify for you on the Day of Resurrection." His uncle said: "If it were not that the Quraysh would reproach me, saying that Abu Talib said it out of fear, I would have said it and cooled your eyes." Thereupon Allah revealed the verse: "Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills."

Bukhari has related the statement of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I myself heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when his uncle was mentioned, say: "Perhaps my intercession will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be placed in a fire up to his ankles, by which his brain will boil." The hadith related by Abu Hurairah establishes that the aforementioned verse was revealed in Makkah concerning Abu Talib.

Tirmidhi and Hakim have related, and Tirmidhi also called this narration hasan, that Ali said: I heard a man praying for the forgiveness of his polytheist parents, so I said: Are you praying for forgiveness for your parents while they were polytheists? He replied: Did not Abraham also pray for the forgiveness of his polytheist father? I mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then the verse "It was not for the Prophet and those who believed to ask forgiveness for the polytheists..." was revealed.

It is possible that this incident also occurred at the time of Abu Talib's death, and both events were causes of the revelation of the aforementioned verse.

Some narrations state that the aforementioned verse was revealed concerning the mother of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Aminah. None of these narrations is authentic, nor are they worthy of being presented against the strong narration mentioned above (in which the revelation of the verse is stated concerning Abu Talib). Therefore, it is necessary not to accept such narrations.

Hakim and Bayhaqi, in Dala'il, have related through Ayyub ibn Hani, on the authority of Masruq, the statement of Ibn Mas'ud: One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went to the graveyard and we went with him. He commanded us to sit down, and we sat. He went among the graves until he reached one grave, and he spoke secretly to the grave for a long time, then rose weeping. Because of his weeping we also began to weep. Then he turned toward us. Umar came forward and submitted: O Messenger of Allah, what caused you to weep? We too began to weep because of your weeping, and we became alarmed. The Messenger (ﷺ) came and sat with us and said: You became alarmed because of my weeping. We said: Yes. He said: The grave in which you saw me speaking secretly is the grave of Aminah bint Wahb. I asked Allah for permission to visit her, and Allah granted permission. Then I asked Allah for permission to pray for her forgiveness, but I was not granted permission, and there were revealed to me two verses from "It was not for the Prophet and those who believed..." The emotion that overcame me because of her was the emotion a child feels for his mother, and that is what made me weep.

Hakim called this hadith sahih, but Dhahabi, in his commentary on the Mustadrak, criticized it and wrote that Ayyub ibn Hani was declared weak by Ibn Ma'in.

Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh have related the statement of Ibn Abbas: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the Battle of Tabuk and set out to perform Umrah, and descended from the pass of Usfan, he halted at the grave of his mother. The rest is the same as what appears in the narration of Ibn Mas'ud. Suyuti said: The chain of this hadith is weak and unreliable.

Baghawi has related, through Abu Hurairah and Buraydah, that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (after the conquest) entered Makkah, he reached the grave of his mother Aminah and stood there waiting for permission from Allah to pray for her forgiveness, until the sun became hot. Thereupon the verse "It was not for the Prophet and those who believed..." was revealed.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Shahin related this hadith with the words of Buraydah that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he went to his mother's grave and sat down there. Ibn Jarir related the narration of Buraydah with the words that Baghawi related. Ibn Sa'd, after mentioning this hadith in his Tabaqat, stated explicitly that it is wrong. The grave of Aminah is in al-Abwa', not in Makkah.

Imam Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh related the statement of Buraydah in this way: I was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I had to stop at Usfan. The Messenger (ﷺ) saw his mother's grave there, immediately performed wudu, prayed, and began to weep. Then he said: I asked my Lord for permission to intercede for her, but I was forbidden. Then Allah revealed: "It was not for the Prophet..." Suyuti said: All the chains (narrations) of this hadith are defective.

Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in his commentary on Bukhari, wrote: Whoever calls the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud sahih does not call it sahih li-dhatihi (sound in itself), but calls it sahih because it has been narrated through these routes. But when I considered these routes, I concluded that all these chains are defective. Besides this, there is another reason why this hadith is defective: it contradicts the narration in the Sahihayn which mentions that this verse was revealed in Makkah at the time of Abu Talib's death.

Baghawi has written that Qatadah narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will pray for the forgiveness of my father in the same way Abraham (peace be upon him) prayed for his father." Thereupon the verse "It was not for the Prophet..." was revealed. This narration is mursal, not authentic; it is weak and contradicts the narration of the Sahihayn.

Therefore, it is not correct to use this verse as evidence to declare the parents of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) polytheists. Suyuti wrote several treatises to prove that the parents of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were believers, indeed he proved the faith of all his forefathers and foremothers up to Adam (peace be upon him). I have summarized all of these and compiled a treatise on this subject titled Taqdis Aba' al-Nabi (ﷺ). There is no room here to discuss this subject in greater detail.

An objection: In the hadith in the Sahihayn, at the time of Abu Talib's death, Abu Jahl said to Abu Talib: Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib? And Abu Talib's final reply was that he was upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib. This indicates that Abd al-Muttalib was a polytheist (so how is it established that all the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) were monotheists?).

Answer: It does not follow from this hadith that Abd al-Muttalib was a polytheist; Abd al-Muttalib was certainly a believer. Ibn Sa'd, in his Tabaqat, related through his special chains that Abd al-Muttalib said to Umm Ayman, the nurse of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O blessed one! Do not neglect my son; I saw him near the lote tree. The People of the Book say that this son of mine is the Prophet of this nation." The matter is that Abd al-Muttalib lived in the Age of Ignorance and was unacquainted with the heavenly laws. That was a period of fatrah, and in a period of fatrah, affirming monotheism alone is sufficient (fatrah is the period in which the law of the previous prophet has been effaced, has become void, the original law has been lost, and a new prophet has not yet come). Abu Jahl knew that Abd al-Muttalib was unacquainted with all the laws, and because of this, he and Abu Talib had the opportunity to form the notion that Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was presenting a new religion contrary to the religion of Abd al-Muttalib, and that his new religion clashed with the religion of Abd al-Muttalib; therefore Abu Talib said that he was upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib.

The prayer of Ibrahim for his father's forgiveness was only because of a promise he had made to him.

By "the father of Ibrahim" is meant Azar. Azar was his uncle; his father's name was Tarakh. The full details have already been given in Surah al-An'am.

Some commentators hold that the pronoun in "wa'adahu" refers to the word "father" (abb), and "iyyahu" refers to Ibrahim. That is, the father had promised Ibrahim that he would become a Muslim, and on this Ibrahim said: "I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness once you become a Muslim." According to most commentators, the subject of "wa'ada" is Ibrahim and "iyyahu" refers to Ibrahim's father. (We have translated according to this view: that Ibrahim, in hope of his father's becoming a Muslim, promised him that he would pray for his forgiveness.) This interpretation is supported by the fact that Allah said: "There is indeed for you a good example in Ibrahim ... except for the saying of Ibrahim to his father, 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you.'" In this verse, following Ibrahim has been commanded, but the prayer for forgiveness that Ibrahim made for his father has been excluded from this general command to follow him; that is, it should not be followed. From this it is established that Ibrahim's father was a polytheist, and despite his polytheism, Ibrahim made a promise to him, in hope that he would become a Muslim, that he would pray to his Lord for his forgiveness.

There is a sound hadith in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Of the generations of the children of Adam (peace be upon him) that have passed, I was sent in the best of them" (meaning my forefathers passed on from generation to generation in the best of generations, and the last generation, which is the best of all, is the generation of my mission). With this hadith being authentic, how can it be said that any disbeliever passed in the lineage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?

"Then when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him" (either by his father dying in a state of disbelief, or by being informed by Allah that he would die a disbeliever). When it became clear to Ibrahim that his father was an enemy of Allah, he expressed his disassociation from him and cut off the prayer for forgiveness.

Some exegetes have written that this verse relates to the Hereafter; that is, in the Hereafter, when it becomes clear to Ibrahim that his father is an enemy of Allah, he will disassociate himself from him. Bukhari narrates through Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection, Ibrahim will meet his father Azar. Azar's face will be dark, dusty and downcast. Ibrahim will say to him: 'Did I not tell you not to disobey me?' The father will reply: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Ibrahim (in the presence of Allah) will submit: 'O my Lord! You promised me that on the day when people are raised, You would not disgrace me. Now what greater disgrace could there be than my father's condition?' Allah will say: 'I have made Paradise forbidden for the disbelievers.' Then it will be commanded: 'O Ibrahim! Look beneath your feet.' Ibrahim will look at his feet and will see a dirt-smeared, shaggy hyena, which will then be seized by its legs and thrown into Hell." In one narration it is further added that Ibrahim will express his disassociation from him.

"Indeed Ibrahim was tender-hearted and forbearing." Truly Ibrahim was gentle in disposition and forbearing in nature. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Awwah is the one who sighs greatly out of fear of Allah (who cries 'oh, oh'). In his life, Ibrahim frequently sighed out of fear of Hell." Some said that one who sighs much because of sins is called awwah. The outcome and essence of both views is the same (that one who sighs much is called awwah, whether out of fear of Allah and dread of Hell or out of apprehension of one's sins). Ata said: "Awwah is one who fears Hell and repents from matters that are displeasing to Allah." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Awwah means one who makes much supplication." Ibn Abbas explained: "The believer who repents much is awwah." Hasan and Qatadah said: "Awwah is one who shows compassion and kindness to the servants of Allah." Mujahid said: "It means one of certainty." Ikrimah said: "This word is from the Abyssinian language, and in Abyssinian it means one who has certainty." Uqbah bin Amir said: "Awwah means one who remembers Allah much." According to Sa'id bin Jubair, awwah is one who travels much. In one narration, Sa'id bin Jubair's saying is that awwah means one who teaches good. Nakha'i said: "Awwah means one of understanding." The Qamus says: "Awwah means one who is certain, or one who supplicates, or one who is compassionate, or one of understanding, or one who has faith. This last meaning is in the Abyssinian language." Abu Ubaidah said: "Awwah means one who cries 'oh, oh' out of fear, who humbly pleads out of certainty, and who keeps to obedience." Zajjaj said: "Abu Ubaidah's statement encompasses all the meanings that are given for awwah." Halim means one who overlooks the harmful conduct of others (forbearing). Ibrahim was forbearing, even though his father had told him that if he did not desist, he would stone him to death; yet Ibrahim said: "Peace be upon you (from Hell); I will ask my Lord to forgive you." Ibn Abbas said: "Halim means chief." The Qamus says: "Hilm means forbearance and wisdom. Halim (the form of the intensive adjective) is derived from hilm." The reason that moved Ibrahim to pray for his father's forgiveness is made clear by this sentence (namely, Ibrahim was awwah and halim, therefore he prayed for his father's forgiveness). Muqatil and Kalbi narrate that some people (from their respective tribes) came into the presence of the Messenger and became Muslims. At that time wine had not yet been prohibited, nor had the command to turn from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah for prayer been revealed. These people went back to their homes in that state after becoming Muslims. After they had left, the prohibition of wine and the change of qiblah were revealed, but they were not informed of it. After some time, when they came again to Madinah and learned of the prohibition of wine and the change of qiblah, they submitted: "O Messenger of Allah! Our path diverged from the religion you were upon (in that intervening period). We used to drink wine and pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis during that time, so we were astray." Upon this, Allah revealed the following verse:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 9, verse 115:

And Allah would never misguide a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should beware of. Meaning: after giving the guidance of Islam, Allah does not declare a people to be misguided, nor will He hold them accountable for any act, until He has explained clearly to them the matters they must avoid, and by adopting which thereafter they would deserve to be declared misguided.

Some scholars said: The Prophet (ﷺ) had said regarding his uncle that he would continue to ask forgiveness for him until he was prohibited from doing so. In this verse, Allah explained the excuse for the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement mentioned (that this statement and the promise of seeking forgiveness were made before the prohibition of praying for forgiveness, and therefore it is not subject to accountability). It has also been said that the intent is to declare excused and not accountable those people who, before the prohibition, prayed for forgiveness for their polytheist forefathers. Mujahid said: In the verse, the ruling about the believers who prayed for forgiveness for the polytheists is mentioned specifically, but the ruling is general (before the revelation of the ruling), covering every act of disobedience and obedience (that is, no act performed before the revelation of the ruling is subject to accountability. This is a general principle; it is not specific to praying for forgiveness for polytheists before the prohibition).

Indeed Allah is All-Knowing of everything. Meaning: Allah knows well who did it out of ignorance and lack of knowledge, and who did it under the influence of rebelliousness and defiance, who deserves to be declared misguided and who does not deserve it; Allah knows these matters well.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides Allah, no protector and no helper.﴾ Certainly, the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone; He gives life and causes death. (O people!) Besides Allah, there is no one who is your supporter, such that he could protect you from Allah, nor any helper, such that he could repel the harm sent by Allah. Therefore, it is not lawful for you to form (heartfelt) friendship with the polytheists and to make supplications for their forgiveness, even if they are your close relatives. For you, the friendship and help of Allah are sufficient.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 9, verse 117:

Allah turned in mercy towards the Prophet and towards the Muhajirun and the Ansar. Allah turned His attention to the condition of the Prophet and to the condition of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. The permission that had been given to the hypocrites not to take part in the jihad of Tabuk, Allah forgave that lapse. Or the meaning is that Allah saved them from being declared sinners, as was said concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿That Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾. Some have said: this is an encouragement to repentance. No one is free of need for repentance, to the extent that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Companions too are in need of repentance. Allah has said: ﴿Turn to Allah in repentance, all of you﴾. The matter is that every person, at whatever rank he may be, falls short of reaching the rank above him (and desires to reach a higher rank), therefore it is necessary for him to repent of the deficiency that is in him. The verse shows the excellence of repentance, that repentance is a special station of the prophets and the righteous. Some have said: in this verse the mention of the Messenger is by way of a preface, because he was the means of the acceptance of the Companions' repentance, so his mention was placed at the beginning as a preface, just as in the verse ﴿And know that a fifth of whatever you acquire belongs to Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near relatives﴾, the mention of Allah is by way of a preface.

﴿Who followed him in the hour of hardship﴾: that is, those who supported the Prophet in a time of such difficulty. That is, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the Muhajirun and the Ansar to the jihad of Tabuk, they followed him. "Sa'ah" means time, and "'usrah" means hardship. In this expedition there was great scarcity and difficulty for the Muslims in mounts, provisions and water, therefore the Tabuk campaign is called Ghazwat al-'Usrah or Ghazwat Jaysh al-'Usrah, and it is also called Ghazwat al-Jaysh. Thus said al-Baghawi.

Hasan said: for every ten men there was only one camel, and the ten men would ride that single camel in turns. One would dismount and another would mount. For provisions there were dates that had become shrivelled and poor-quality barley. Whatever was with them, the people would divide among themselves. Then the situation reached the point where some people, due to extreme hunger, would take a single date and turn it in their mouths, and when they had enjoyed its taste, they would give it to their companion, and he would suck it, then drink a mouthful of water on top of it. In this way all the people would suck one date in turns, and by the time of sucking it the date would be finished, leaving only the stone. Yet with faith and certainty they would walk on with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Imam Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim narrated on the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab that Umar said: We set out towards Tabuk in the days of intense heat (accompanying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)). We halted at one stopping place and thirst struck us so severely that we thought our necks would break. Some people would go in search of water, and it was assumed that they would not return alive. Some would slaughter their camel, extract water from its stomach, squeeze it and drink it, and whatever remained they would place on their liver. Abu Bakr said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Allah has made you accustomed to good supplication (that is, you make supplications for good and Allah accepts your supplication). Pray to Allah for us. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: Do you like this? Abu Bakr said: Yes. The Messenger (ﷺ) raised both his hands towards the sky, and before he could bring them down, clouds rose and covered the army. Then so much rain fell that they filled whatever vessels the people had. After that, when we went out to see where the rain had fallen, we found that beyond the army no rain had fallen.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Abu Hurrah al-Ansari that the people (on the road to Tabuk) halted at al-Hijr. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered: No one should take the water here. Then, after departing, they halted at another stopping place. No one had water, and the people complained of having no water. The Messenger (ﷺ) prayed two rak'ahs and made supplication, and Allah immediately sent a cloud, from which so much rain fell that all were satisfied. An Ansari said to his companion, whom the people considered a hypocrite: Look! By the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah has sent rain upon us. He said: The rain has come because of such-and-such stars (their rising and their movement). Thereupon Allah revealed the verse: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it﴾.

﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾: that is, after the hearts of a group among them had begun to waver. "Qulub fariq" means the hearts of some people. By "zaygh" it is not meant that the hearts of some people had turned away from religion, but rather that they inclined towards not going forward and returning because of the extreme hardships. This is what "zaygh" means.

Al-Kalbi said: some people had intended not to go along, but (after reflection) they caught up with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from behind. Ibn Ishaq and Muhammad ibn Umar report that the intentions of some Muslims slackened and they were left behind from going with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), (and the time passed while they kept saying "soon, soon"), yet these people had no hesitation about going (they wanted to go and intended to go, but got caught up in procrastination). Among them were Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' and Abu Dharr al-Ghifari. This group was truly faithful; no one had any doubt about their Islam. Ibn Ishaq related the report of Ibn Mas'ud that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out, some people (on the way) left his company and began to return. The Companions would say: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! So-and-so has left us. The Messenger (ﷺ) would say: Leave him. If there is any good in his (coming along), Allah will bring him to you from behind, otherwise I will await Allah's command concerning him (I will do what Allah commands). Finally, when Abu Dharr fell behind, the people said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Abu Dharr has fallen behind, his camel has become sluggish. The Messenger (ﷺ), as usual, gave the same first answer. Abu Dharr scolded the camel, but the camel remained sluggish (there was no speed in its pace). Seeing this, Abu Dharr hoisted his baggage on his back and walked on foot, step by step, behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Muhammad ibn Umar reports that Abu Dharr used to say: I fell behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk because of my camel. The camel was very weak and emaciated. I thought that I would feed it fodder for a few days, and then I would quickly catch up with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from behind. So I kept feeding it for a few days, then set out and reached Dhu al-Marwah when the camel lay down. I laboured over it the whole day, but it did not move from its place. Finally I loaded my baggage upon myself and set off, and at midday I reached a place from where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) could be seen. A Muslim among those travelling saw me and said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! This man is walking alone on foot. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: May it be Abu Dharr. The people looked at me closely and said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! By Allah, it is indeed Abu Dharr.
